articles.title: 'Hand of unity' vs 'unhinged incitement': Likud, Eisenkot trade barbs over Netanyahu's offer
articles.summary: Israel's ruling Likud Party has accused opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot of making inflammatory remarks against caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
articles.body: Israel's ruling Likud Party has accused opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot of making inflammatory remarks against caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his office, describing his statements as "unhinged incitement".The party also questioned allegations surrounding Netanyahu's chief of staff.In a post on X, Likud criticised Eisenkot for making provocative remarks despite Netanyahu's invitation to join hands and form a national unity government."Gadi Eisenkot’s unhinged incitement against Prime Minister Netanyahu and his office is appalling. While the prime minister extends a hand of unity, Eisenkot and his colleagues issue inflammatory, incendiary statements every day in venomous language," the party said.Defending Netanyahu's chief of staff, Likud said the official had fulfilled his obligations by informing the police about suspected serious criminal activity."Eisenkot is inciting against the chief of staff, a law-abiding citizen who passed information to the police about suspected serious criminal activity, as he was obligated to do," the party said.The ruling party also questioned the allegations against the official, asking, "Did the chief of staff plant the envelopes of cash with the suspects? The absurdity of Eisenkot’s unhinged incitement is outrageous."The exchange comes amid growing political tensions between Netanyahu and Eisenkot over the formation of Israel's next government and allegations linked to the Prime Minister's Office.Netanyahu had earlier invited Eisenkot to hold negotiations without preconditions to form a national unity government, arguing that Israel needed a broad political coalition to tackle its security challenges, particularly the threat from Iran.In a video statement, Netanyahu said his recent conversation with Eisenkot had strengthened his belief in the need for a broad-based government. He argued that a narrow coalition, or one dependent on parties he described as supporters of terrorism, would be unable to address the country's security challenges.Netanyahu also urged political leaders to set aside their differences and proposed resolving the issue of military conscription through discussions involving representatives of the Haredi community.However, Eisenkot, who leads the Yashar party, rejected the proposal, calling Netanyahu's overture "another spin". He said negotiating teams from Likud and Yesh Atid had already scheduled a meeting.Eisenkot also maintained that any national emergency government formed under his leadership would have to accept his proposed principles and break away from extremist political forces.The political standoff follows last month's election, in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority. Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot the mandate to form a government last week.Meanwhile, finance minister and Religious Zionism Party chairman Bezalel Smotrich backed Netanyahu's appeal for unity, urging Eisenkot to accept the proposal and describing it as an opportunity to demonstrate national responsibility.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial in March 2027 over murder of three children
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in January 2023, will face a second trial on March 29, 2027,
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in January 2023, will face a second trial on March 29, 2027, after her first trial ended in a mistrial earlier this year.According to the New York Post, prosecutors from Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz’s office said on Monday that they were prepared to proceed with a jury trial against the 36-year-old, although they did not explicitly confirm whether they would pursue the same first-degree murder charges.Clancy’s defence lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he understood the prosecution's position to mean that it intended to proceed with the first-degree murder indictments she faced in the previous trial.“I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it’s an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree indictments, so we will pick a trial date,” Reddington said.Judge William Sullivan set March 29 as the trial date, overriding the prosecution's objection. Prosecutors had sought to push the proceedings until May, citing scheduling conflicts.The first trial, which lasted several weeks over the summer, ended in September after the 12-member jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The BBC reported that the mistrial followed a deadlock over the charges.A week before the latest hearing, Sullivan rejected a defence bid to dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds, clearing the way for prosecutors to bring Clancy to trial again.Clancy is accused of killing her three children on January 24, 2023. She does not deny killing them, but her defence team argues that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors maintain that the killings were intentional.She is currently being held at a state-run psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts. Her lawyer had previously indicated that he would consider a plea deal if prosecutors agreed that she could remain in psychiatric care rather than be sent to prison.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oprah Winfrey packed a care bag and wrote a personal note for a woman she may never meet, joining an Australian charity drive that has collected over 1.1 million bags and now hopes to gather 150,000 more
articles.summary: A parcel sent from the United States has become part of an Australian Christmas charity campaign after television host Oprah Winfrey packed a care bag for
articles.body: A parcel sent from the United States has become part of an Australian Christmas charity campaign after television host Oprah Winfrey packed a care bag for a stranger and included a handwritten note. According to a media release from Bunnings Australia, Winfrey took part in Share the Dignity's annual It's in the Bag appeal, which runs across Australia from 6 to 22 November 2026. The campaign encourages people to fill a new or pre-loved handbag, backpack or tote with everyday essentials, period products and a personal message. The packed bags can then be dropped off at a local Bunnings store. The campaign supports women and girls facing homelessness, domestic violence and financial hardship. This year, the charity hopes to collect 150,000 bags to meet growing demand from its registered charity partners.A personal note from across the PacificShare the Dignity Founder and Managing Director Rochelle Courtenay invited Winfrey to join the campaign after meeting her at an event in Australia and explaining the charity's work. Winfrey later packed a bag in the United States and sent it to Australia. She also included a handwritten 'Dear Her' note for the woman who would eventually receive it. "I'll admit I let out a squeal when the bag arrived," Courtenay said in the Bunnings release. "But what stays with me is the note. Oprah has written to a woman she will probably never meet. That is what Australians have been doing for eleven years: one woman saying to another, I don't know you, but I thought of you."Courtenay explained that Winfrey's donation would be distributed in exactly the same way as every other bag collected through the campaign. "Oprah's bag will do what every other bag does. It will go to one woman who needs it. It carries the same message as a bag packed by a grandmother in Toowoomba or a family in Darwin: you are seen, you matter, someone cares," Courtenay stated.Ten years of community collectionsNovember 2026 marks 10 years since Share the Dignity partnered with hardware retailer Bunnings to provide collection points across Australia. During this period, Australians have donated more than 1.1 million bags through the campaign. In 2025, people handed in 123,295 bags at physical collection points. Online donations also helped pay for more than 30,000 additional bags. "You don't have to register or attend an event," Courtenay said. "You can simply pack a bag, take it to Bunnings, and we get it into the hands of someone who needs it."Melissa O'Neill, Bunnings Chief Corporate Affairs Officer, said in the company's announcement that employees, customers and local communities had supported the campaign for a decade. "For 10 years, our team members, customers and communities have embraced Share the Dignity's It's in the Bag appeal, helping provide essential items and a message of care to women and girls experiencing homelessness, domestic violence or financial hardship," O'Neill said. "Every bag represents a simple act of kindness that can make a meaningful difference to someone at a difficult time, which is why this appeal continues to resonate so strongly with our teams and customers."She encouraged people to visit participating stores and donate before the campaign ends on 22 November. "We encourage anyone who can, to pack a bag and drop it into a participating Bunnings store between 6 and 22 November, helping remind someone they're not alone this Christmas," O'Neill added.Rising demand and lived experienceThe target of 150,000 bags comes as support services across Australia face growing demand. Figures from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, cited by Bunnings, show that nearly 289,000 people received support from specialist homelessness services across the country in 2024-25. Of these, 17,063 women and children affected by family violence experienced ongoing homelessness. This was higher than the 15,510 recorded in 2022-23.For people receiving the donations, the bags can provide practical help during some of the most difficult periods of their lives. One recipient, Lenna Boxall, received a donated bag while undergoing treatment for breast cancer, major surgery, chronic pain and medical menopause. At the same time, she was caring for her three daughters and two nieces, whose mother had fled domestic violence. "It was a really, really big, incredible thing at the time, receiving a bag. It just made me feel seen and cared about. I just really appreciated that people cared enough to want to help," Boxall said in the release. "I'm strong and I'm tough, but I'm also human and I'm an emotional person and I feel a lot... I'm learning it's ok for me to accept help."How the public can take partCourtenay founded Share the Dignity in 2015 after learning that women experiencing homelessness were sometimes unable to afford basic sanitary products during their periods. Since then, the charity has grown with the support of more than 2,500 volunteers across Australia and has distributed over six million packets of period products. "We don't need 150,000 Oprahs," Courtenay said. "We need 150,000 Australians willing to care about someone they may never meet. Find a handbag, backpack or tote you no longer use. Fill it with the essentials, add something lovely, and write a Dear Her note. That note may be the most important thing you put inside." People can drop off their completed bags at participating Bunnings stores until 22 November 2026. Those who cannot visit a store can also support the campaign by funding a bag online through Share the Dignity's website.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.standfirst: Trabalhos abordam a importância da odontologia para a sociedade e como novas tecnologias humanizam os atendimentos.
articles.summary: Trabalhos abordam a importância da odontologia para a sociedade e como novas tecnologias humanizam os atendimentos.
articles.body:
Grupo Asa Branca — Foto: Reprodução / TV Asa Branca

O Grupo Asa Branca é finalista no 3º Prêmio CRO-PE de Jornalismo. O resultado foi divulgado na noite da segunda-feira (18) por meio das redes sociais do Conselho Regional de Odontologia. Os trabalhos concorrem nas categorias online, televisão, videocast e rádio.

A divulgação dos resultados dos vencedores será realizada na próxima quinta-feira (26), em um evento promovido pelo Conselho.

Confira os trabalhos finalistas por categorias

Na categoria online, os jornalistas Fábio Gomes e Larissa Juliana concorrem com a reportagem “ Pré-natal odontológico: entenda por que cuidar dos dentes também protege mãe e bebê ”, publicada no g1 Caruaru e região.

Na categoria televisão, o jornalista Joel Almeida concorre com a reportagem “ Inclusão da odontologia: novas tecnologias e humanização melhoram o sorriso de neurodivergentes ”. O portal CNF também concorre com a matéria “ Bruxismo: quando o corpo reage ao estado da mente ”, de Natália Rodrigues e Mariana Granja.

Os jornalistas Magno Wendel, Jessé Aciole e Letícia Loura concorrem com a reportagem “ Inovação na odontologia – A tecnologia ajudando a cuidar dos sorrisos ”, veiculada na CBN Caruaru.

articles.title: Talibã censura até o críquete no Afeganistão | G1
articles.standfirst: Regime proíbe rádios de transmitir notícias sobre o esporte mais popular do país e mantém mulheres afastadas das quadras, das escolas e da vida pública, submetidas a um sistema de repressão.
articles.summary: Regime proíbe rádios de transmitir notícias sobre o esporte mais popular do país e mantém mulheres afastadas das quadras, das escolas e da vida pública, submetidas a um sistema de repressão.
articles.body:
Soldados do Talibã comemoram um ano da saída dos Estados Unidos do Afeganistão — Foto: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP

O regime Talibã, que há cinco anos retomou o controle do Afeganistão, proibiu as estações de rádio de Kandahar de transmitir reportagens e comentários sobre o críquete, o esporte mais popular do país. O esporte não está proibido, mas a medida priva os torcedores de receberem informações básicas relacionadas ao críquete, como os resultados das partidas.

O veto às rádios, antecipado pela agência de notícias AFP, ocorre às vésperas do relançamento da Premier League do Afeganistão, em dezembro nos Emirados Árabes Unidos. O torneio terá a participação de cinco equipes e foi autorizada pelo Talibã.

A transmissão dos jogos pela TV já havia sido extinta, restando às rádios a única opção de transmissão. Por enquanto, a proibição parece estar limitada a Kandahar, no Sul do país, onde nasceu o líder talibã, Hibatullah Akhundzada. Os motivos não foram explicados.

Chefe do Talibã, Mawlawi Hibatullah Akhundzada, em foto sem data — Foto: Talibã/AFP

Desde que assumiu o governo, o regime permitiu a prática do críquete apenas para os homens. Impedidas de jogar, as atletas da equipe feminina fugiram do país e se exilaram na Austrália, onde formaram um time de refugiadas.

Em julho passado, elas foram reconhecidas pelo Conselho Internacional de Críquete, que anunciou financiamento para a equipe e a promessa de disputar eventos classificatórios até 2030.

A situação dramática das mulheres afegãs foi descrita como "apartheid de gênero" pela ONG Human Rights Watch. Elas foram proibidas de frequentar escolas, praticar esportes e ocupar cargos públicos. O Talibã impôs mais de 230 decretos, que retiram os seus direitos básicos, como o acesso à educação e à liberdade de movimento. Também não podem falar em público, cantar ou ler em voz alta.

A fundadora do Arquivo de Justiça do Afeganistão, Metra Mehran, classifica as restrições como um "um sistema de opressão de gênero institucionalizado". Segundo ela, o Código de Processo Penal formalizou a discriminação e legitimou a violência contra as mulheres .

A Human Rights Watch considera que este código deixa as sobreviventes de abusos sem acesso à Justiça e desmantela ainda mais as proteções para mulheres. A idade mínima para o casamento de meninas, por exemplo, foi eliminada.

articles.title: Cuiabá sanciona lei que prevê ensino religioso confessional nas escola | G1
articles.standfirst: Disciplina será facultativa para alunos do ensino fundamental e participação deverá ser autorizada pelos pais ou responsáveis no momento da matrícula.
articles.summary: Disciplina será facultativa para alunos do ensino fundamental e participação deverá ser autorizada pelos pais ou responsáveis no momento da matrícula.
articles.body:
A Prefeitura de Cuiabá sancionou uma lei que regulamenta a oferta de ensino religioso nas escolas da rede pública municipal. A publicação foi feita no Diário Oficial de sexta-feira (13). O projeto é de autoria do vereador Rafael Ranalli (PL), e foi apresentado e aprovado no início deste mês.

Pela nova legislação, o ensino religioso será uma disciplina de oferta obrigatória nos horários normais das escolas municipais de ensino fundamental, mas a matrícula será facultativa . A participação deverá ser autorizada pelos pais ou responsáveis no momento da matrícula .

A lei estabelece que os alunos que não optarem pelas aulas deverão receber atividades pedagógicas complementares, como reforço nas disciplinas em que apresentarem menor rendimento acadêmico. A escolha também não poderá resultar em qualquer tipo de discriminação, favorecimento ou prejuízo à trajetória escolar dos estudantes.

O texto determina ainda que as aulas sejam ministradas por professores com registro no Ministério da Educação (MEC), preferencialmente integrantes do quadro efetivo do magistério municipal, e credenciados por uma autoridade religiosa competente .

Conforme a legislação, o conteúdo programático ficará sob responsabilidade das diferentes entidades religiosas. O município deverá apoiar a organização das atividades e garantir que sejam respeitados os princípios constitucionais.

O credenciamento das instituições religiosas deverá ocorrer de forma igualitária, garantindo pluralismo e respeito às diferentes tradições de fé.

A legislação também autoriza a Prefeitura a realizar concurso público específico para contratar professores de ensino religioso. Os profissionais aprovados deverão receber remuneração nos mesmos padrões aplicados aos demais integrantes do magistério municipal.

articles.title: Grupo suspeito de vender drogas por delivery movimentou R$ 2,3 milhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Polícia cumpriu mandados de busca e apreensão e prisão preventiva em Palmas e Luzimangues. Investigação começou após denúncia anônima sobre venda de cocaína na região sul da capital.
articles.summary: Polícia cumpriu mandados de busca e apreensão e prisão preventiva em Palmas e Luzimangues. Investigação começou após denúncia anônima sobre venda de cocaína na região sul da capita
articles.body:
Grupo suspeito de manter laboratório industrial de crack teria movimentado R$ 2,3 milhões com tráfico — Foto: Divulgação

Quatro pessoas foram presas na manhã desta terça-feira (17), suspeitas de participar de um grupo que mantinha um laboratório industrial de crack em uma chácara de Palmas . Segundo a polícia, o grupo chegou a movimentar R$ 2,3 milhões. Além das prisões, também foram cumpridos 12 mandados de busca e apreensão.

Os nomes dos suspeitos não foram divulgados, por isso o g1 não conseguiu contato com as defesas deles.

Conforme apurado pela TV Anhanguera, foram expedidos nove mandados de prisão preventiva, sendo que quatro foram cumpridos nesta manhã. Durante a ação, também houve três prisões em flagrante, totalizando sete pessoas detidas na Operação Fim de Linha.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

Os mandados foram cumpridos em Palmas e Luzimangues, distrito de Porto Nacional. Os documentos foram expedidos pelo juiz da Vara das Garantias, Milton Lamenha.

De acordo com a polícia, a distribuição das drogas funcionava quase como um delivery. Para as entregas, era cobrada uma taxa de R$ 30 a R$ 50 dos compradores, que era paga via Pix. Os comprovantes dessas taxas foram decisivos para a polícia identificar os distribuidores do grupo.

As investigações apontaram que o comandante do grupo era um homem conhecido como “Naldinho” e “Arthur”, chamado pelos comparsas de “Compadre”. Conforme a polícia, ele comprava a matéria-prima, mandava refinar, controlava o estoque e definia para quem vender.

O caso passou a ser investigado em fevereiro deste ano, após uma denúncia anônima de que um homem estaria vendendo cocaína na região sul de Palmas, com entregas de carro. Durante uma abordagem em Taquaralto, o suspeito teria jogado uma caixa com dois tabletes de crack pela janela.

Logo depois, os policiais encontraram o laboratório onde a droga era produzida. A estrutura funcionava como uma fábrica e continha prensa hidráulica, balanças de precisão, liquidificadores industriais, moldes para tabletes, insumos químicos e cadernos com a contabilidade do tráfico. No local foram apreendidos mais de 5 kg de cocaína, entre pó e pasta-base prensada, 373,47 g de tetracaína, insumo para adulterar a droga, e 58 munições de vários calibres.

Os valores das vendas passavam pela conta bancária da companheira de Naldinho. Entre setembro de 2023 e janeiro de 2026, ela chegou a movimentar R$ 2.302.671, mesmo declarando ser vendedora com renda de R$ 1,5 mil por mês, de acordo com relatório do Conselho de Controle de Atividades Financeiras.

A polícia também identificou que a mulher teria enviado R$ 80.620 em Pix fracionados ao suspeito conhecido Maguila, entre junho de 2025 e outubro de 2026. Maguila foi preso em junho de 2026 durante a Operação Nocaute, da Denac.

Na época, a polícia informou que Maguila ostentava uma vida de luxo, frequentando restaurantes caros sem possuir emprego formal, enquanto coordenava a distribuição de drogas no varejo.

articles.title: Rússia ataca infraestrutura da Ucrânia, e Kiev atinge ponte que liga Crimeia ao território russo | G1
articles.standfirst: Pontes Norte e Sul foram atingidas durante ofensiva contra a capital ucraniana, segundo o prefeito. Sistema de metrô também foi parcialmente danificado.
articles.summary: Pontes Norte e Sul foram atingidas durante ofensiva contra a capital ucraniana, segundo o prefeito. Sistema de metrô também foi parcialmente danificado.
articles.body:
A Rússia lançou uma ofensiva contra infraestruturas da Ucrânia nesta terça-feira (17) e derrubou duas pontes sobre o rio Dnipro, na capital Kiev, e instalações de energia em outras regiões do país. Em resposta, forças ucranianas realizaram um ataque contra a Ponte da Crimeia, que liga a península anexada por Moscou ao território russo.

O presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelensky , classificou a operação contra a ponte como "sem precedentes". Segundo ele, o ataque foi uma resposta aos bombardeios russos contra a infraestrutura ucraniana.

A Ponte da Crimeia, também conhecida como Ponte de Kerch, foi atingida pelo segundo dia consecutivo. A estrutura é considerada estratégica para o transporte de pessoas, mercadorias e equipamentos militares entre a Rússia e a península, anexada por Moscou em 2014.

Na capital ucraniana, os ataques russos atingiram as pontes Norte e Sul, que passam sobre o rio Dnipro. Segundo o prefeito de Kiev, Vitali Klitschko, as duas estruturas sofreram danos e foram interditadas ao tráfego

Os bombardeios também danificaram parte do sistema de metrô e instalações de infraestrutura crítica. O fornecimento de água e aquecimento foi interrompido em alguns bairros da cidade.

A ofensiva russa atingiu ainda instalações de energia na região de Dnipropetrovsk, no centro da Ucrânia. Segundo a DTEK, maior empresa privada de energia do país, cerca de 700 mil residências ficaram sem eletricidade.

Os danos afetaram a cidade de Dnipro e outros distritos da região. Autoridades locais também relataram ataques contra Kharkiv e Zaporizhzhia. Na região de Cherkasy, três pessoas ficaram feridas.

O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia confirmou os ataques às pontes de Kiev e afirmou que a ofensiva teve como alvos instalações de transporte, militares e de energia.

Imagem divulgada em 17 de novembro de 2026 no canal oficial do presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelensky, no Telegram, mostra danos à Ponte da Crimeia, também conhecida como Ponte de Kerch, que liga a península à Rússia. Zelensky afirmou nesta terça-feira que Kiev realizou um ataque "sem precedentes" contra a estrutura. Segundo o presidente ucraniano, a operação foi uma resposta aos ataques russos contra a infraestrutura do país. — Foto: Oleksandr Gimanov / AFP

Rússia diz ter derrubado 1.441 drones ucranianos

Em meio à troca de ataques, o Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que suas forças de defesa antiaérea derrubaram 1.441 drones ucranianos durante a noite.

Segundo Moscou, os aparelhos foram interceptados em mais de 20 regiões russas, incluindo Moscou, Belgorod, Volgogrado e Vladimir, além da Crimeia.

O número é o segundo maior registro diário desde o início do ano, de acordo com um levantamento da agência France-Presse (AFP) baseado em comunicados oficiais russos.

Rússia rejeita entrada da Ucrânia na Otan

Nesta terça-feira, o vice-ministro das Relações Exteriores da Rússia, Sergei Ryabkov, voltou a rejeitar a possibilidade de a Ucrânia integrar a Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte (Otan).

Segundo a agência de notícias Interfax, Ryabkov afirmou que Moscou se opõe categoricamente à entrada dos ucranianos na aliança militar.

O diplomata também disse que ainda não há acordo sobre a data ou o local da próxima rodada de negociações para um possível acordo de paz entre os dois países.

A entrada do país na aliança militar é um dos principais pontos de divergência entre Moscou e Kiev.

O governo russo considera a possibilidade uma ameaça à sua segurança e usa a expansão da Otan como uma das justificativas para a invasão do território ucraniano, iniciada em fevereiro de 2022.

A Ucrânia, por sua vez, defende a adesão à aliança como uma forma de garantir sua segurança diante de novas agressões russas.

Em meio às negociações, Zelensky afirmou na semana passada que os Estados Unidos levantaram a possibilidade de a Ucrânia retirar suas tropas de áreas de Donbas, no leste do país, que ainda não estão sob controle russo, em troca da entrada na Otan .

Zelensky, no entanto, disse que Kiev não abrirá mão de seu território. Ele também alertou que Moscou pode usar as negociações para enfraquecer a aliança militar e tentar alterar as fronteiras europeias.

articles.title: US tightens AI chip curbs: How Trump plans to block China's indirect access to American technology
articles.summary: The Trump administration has introduced new export control rules to prevent China and other restricted countries from gaining indirect access to advanced
articles.body: The Trump administration has introduced new export control rules to prevent China and other restricted countries from gaining indirect access to advanced American artificial intelligence (AI) chips and computing power through overseas data centres.The rules, announced by the US Commerce Department on Monday, seek to close loopholes that allow Chinese companies to rent computing capacity powered by American technology from facilities located in third countries. The restrictions took effect immediately.The move comes amid growing concerns in Washington that existing export controls are insufficient to prevent China from accessing advanced US chips through cloud computing services and data centres in Southeast Asia.“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said while announcing the new restrictions.Under the rules, overseas data centres providing services to companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba will be required to identify their end users. Additional licensing requirements will also apply to chip sales involving Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the rules identify as countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorised destinations.Why is the US tightening AI chip restrictions?The US has imposed restrictions on exports of its most advanced AI chips to China to maintain its technological advantage in the global artificial intelligence race.However, American lawmakers and policymakers have raised concerns that Chinese companies could bypass these restrictions by accessing computing power remotely through cloud services.Under existing rules, restrictions primarily focus on the physical export of advanced chips. This has created concerns that companies in restricted countries could rent processing capacity from data centres located in countries where American chips can be legally deployed.Last year, US Representative Michael Lawler, a Republican from New York, introduced legislation seeking to expand export controls to cover remote access to advanced computing technology.He told Congress that “physical export controls” under existing rules do not cover remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” US export restrictions.The bill has passed the House of Representatives, while lawmakers in the Senate are also pursuing measures to tighten restrictions.These proposals include allowing Congress to review licences for advanced AI chip sales to China, requiring the Commerce Department to track chips to prevent their diversion to unauthorised destinations, and pushing US allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to align their export restrictions with Washington.Megaspeed controversy puts export controls under scrutinyThe latest restrictions come amid scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US export controls.The company provides computing power to Chinese businesses using chips installed in data centres across Southeast Asia, including facilities in Malaysia.Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced criticism after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department had been late in imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports linked to Megaspeed.President Donald Trump acknowledged tensions between the Treasury and Commerce departments over the issue on Monday. He suggested Lutnick may have delayed imposing restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile US-China relationship.“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.The controversy has also drawn attention to the role of Southeast Asian countries in the supply chain for advanced AI computing infrastructure.Singapore confirmed last week that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia that might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”Malaysia has also launched an investigation into whether chips imported into the country were subsequently re-exported to other destinations in violation of applicable restrictions.“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.Trump heads to Asia amid fragile trade truceThe new restrictions were announced on the same day Trump departed for an Asian tour, during which he is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year.The meeting comes as Washington and Beijing attempt to maintain a fragile trade truce amid continuing tensions over technology, tariffs and access to critical supply chains.The latest rules underline Washington's efforts to prevent China from accessing advanced American computing technology, even through third-country data centres, as competition between the two countries over artificial intelligence intensifies.You use AI every day. articles.title: Michael J. Fox founded his Parkinson's research charity in 2000; its November 14 gala raised $6 million, while the foundation has directed more than $2.5 billion toward research over 25 years
articles.summary: Michael J. Fox's Parkinson's research charity gala raised a record $6 million, continuing a 25-year legacy of funding over $2.5 billion for Parkinson's research. Discover the impact and future goals of The Michael J. Fox Foundation.
articles.body: A fundraising event for Parkinson's research brought together actor Michael J. Fox, his wife and their three daughters in New York on November 14. The annual gathering marked another milestone for an organisation that the actor established after receiving his own Parkinson's diagnosis. According to USA TODAY, the event reportedly raised a record $6 million, adding to the foundation's efforts to support scientific research, improve treatments and work towards finding a cure for the neurological condition.According to The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research's official website, the organisation has deployed more than $2.5 billion towards research during its first 25 years. Founded in 2000, the charity has become the world's largest nonprofit funder of Parkinson's research. Its latest fundraising event, titled 'A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson's', took place at the Waldorf Astoria in New York and brought together entertainers, supporters and members of Fox's family.Michael J. Fox attended gala with wife and daughtersFox, 65, attended the November 14 event with his wife, Tracy Pollan, and their three daughters, Esmé, 25, and twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, 31. Their appearance together attracted attention, as the family rarely makes public appearances as a group. The couple also have a son, Sam, 37, who was not present at the event. According to USA TODAY's report, the fundraiser featured musical performances by John Mayer and Brad Paisley, comedy appearances and several celebrity guests. Comedian Denis Leary hosted the evening, while performers and supporters came together to raise money for Parkinson's research.The event also featured a performance involving Fox, Mayer, members of Super Soul Banned and No Doubt guitarist Tom Dumont, who had publicly shared his early-onset Parkinson's diagnosis earlier in 2026. The gala was particularly significant for Fox and Pollan, who have spent decades supporting research into the condition. Speaking to PEOPLE at the event, Pollan said the money raised goes towards supporting scientists and their work. She also described the progress made through the foundation's long-running efforts.Fox established foundation after Parkinson's diagnosisFox was diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson's disease in 1991, when he was 29 years old. The actor initially kept his diagnosis private before publicly disclosing it in 1998. Two years after publicly disclosing his diagnosis, he established The Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000 to accelerate research and improve the lives of people living with the condition.Parkinson's is a progressive neurological disorder that affects movement. It develops when nerve cells responsible for producing dopamine, a chemical involved in controlling movement, become damaged or die. Common symptoms include tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement and difficulties with balance and coordination.Through his foundation, Fox sought to bring greater attention and funding to a condition that affects millions of people worldwide. The organisation supports research into the causes of Parkinson's, potential treatments, early detection and approaches that could eventually lead to a cure.Foundation reports more than $2.5 billion in research fundingThe foundation's official 'Your Gift Powers Progress' update highlights the scale of its work over the past 25 years. It states that the organisation has deployed more than $2.5 billion towards Parkinson's research since its establishment in 2000.The foundation also reports that treatment options have increased by 200 per cent since its launch, while nearly two dozen treatments have been approved over the past decade. Its work brings together researchers, medical professionals, pharmaceutical companies and people living with Parkinson's. The organisation also supports clinical studies and makes research resources available to encourage collaboration and accelerate scientific progress. For 2026, the foundation said it aimed to fund $600 million in research, reflecting its continued commitment to advancing discoveries and improving treatment options.The November 14 gala marked the 26th year of the fundraising tradition. For Fox, the event represented more than a celebrity gathering or an annual fundraising milestone. It reflected the continuing efforts of researchers, donors, families and people living with Parkinson's to move closer to better treatments and, ultimately, a cure.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Michigan man sued his brother and sister-in-law over alleged irregularities in their mother's estate; his lawsuit was dismissed and a November 13 appeals court upheld $11,000 in fees awarded against him
articles.summary: A Michigan family feud over an inheritance has become costly, after a son who questioned how his brother handled their late mother’s finances was ordered
articles.body: A Michigan family feud over an inheritance has become costly, after a son who questioned how his brother handled their late mother’s finances was ordered to pay $11,000 in legal fees. The Michigan Court of Appeals has now upheld the award, deciding that while parts of the lawsuit had questionable legal merit, the original allegations were not entirely without foundation. The November 13, 2026 ruling is an example of how disputes over the administration of an estate can result in protracted legal battles and significant financial costs whether or not claims are ultimately brought to trial.An unequal inheritance sparks a family disputeThe case concerned Frieda Mae Chapman, who died in November 2021, after the death of her husband Leonard Chapman in April 2017. The Michigan Court of Appeals said Frieda had three sons, Glenn Chapman, who received 20% of her estate; Kurt Chapman, who received 37%; and Christopher Chapman, who received 40%.Christopher had handled much of his mother’s finances in the last few years of her life, acting as trustee of her trust and having power of attorney. Glenn then asked how those duties had been fulfilled, and filed probate proceedings concerning both his mother’s estate and trust.Allegations over family money handlingThe fight continued in October 2023 when Glenn filed a separate civil suit against Christopher and his wife, Jaime Chapman. Glenn claimed his brother had abused his position of financial authority to derive personal benefits from Frieda’s money, according to Michigan Court of Appeals records.The lawsuit alleged eight claims, including breach of fiduciary duty, embezzlement, conversion, undue influence, conspiracy, unjust enrichment, quantum meruit and fraud.Christopher and Jaime denied the allegations and sought to dismiss the proceedings. The trial court first disposed of two claims and afforded Glenn the chance to amend his complaint. But the litigation continued with more motions and discovery disputes.Finally, in January 2025, Glenn moved to dismiss the case with prejudice, claiming he lacked the funds to pay his attorneys.Lawyer fees battlegroundChristopher and Jaime sought a large legal fee after Glenn dropped the suit. Christopher wanted $37,352.10, Jaime $46,467.50. Their requests increased to $41,772.10 and $47,922.50.In May 2025, the probate court dismissed the complaint and ordered each defendant to pay $5,500 in attorney fees and costs, totaling $11,000.The Michigan Court of Appeals noted that the lower court did not find the lawsuit to be frivolous in its entirety, nor did it find that it was filed primarily to harass or injure the defendants. It did, however, find that Glenn should have realized earlier that the litigation was getting off on the wrong foot.Appeals court denies request for higher paymentsChristopher and Jaime appealed the $11,000 award, saying the original complaint was frivolous and they should be reimbursed for their entire legal bill.But the Michigan Court of Appeals saw it differently. The appellate panel, in its Nov. 13 decision, said the lower court did not clearly err in concluding the lawsuit was not frivolous when it was filed.The court recognized that certain claims were legally quite weak, especially those concerning embezzlement and conversion. It also found some of the allegations against Jaime were less compelling because she was not in a formal fiduciary position over Frieda’s finances.But the judges found the main allegation about Christopher’s fiduciary duties to be reasonable. The proceedings heard evidence including financial records which showed that money from accounts associated with Frieda and her late husband had been used for some personal expenses.The Michigan Court of Appeals also considered the likelihood that Christopher had used his position of trust to influence financial decisions that affected his mother. It said that these facts gave Glenn sufficient reason to proceed with the main accusations even if the allegations were never litigated.The $11,000 prize standsIn dismissing the appeal, the Michigan Court of Appeals drew a distinction between a lawsuit that fails and one that is legally frivolous. Michigan law provides that a claim may be deemed frivolous if it is filed primarily to harass someone, if there is no reasonable factual basis for the claim, or if the claim lacks any arguable legal merit.But the appellate judges found that the original lawsuit as a whole didn’t rise to that level. But they also found no reason to overturn the trial court's decision to award $11,000 for legal expenses incurred in the later stages of the legal proceedings.The Nov. 13 ruling keeps the original fee awards in place. Christopher and Jaime keep their original $5,500 awards against Glenn.The ruling does not settle whether Christopher mishandled his mother’s finances or resolve the underlying allegations of financial wrongdoing. However, it does not address the legal basis for the award of fees, and it further supports the distinction between unsuccessful litigation and proceedings that meet the frivolous standard under Michigan law.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: At COP31, Nepal pushes for billions to help disaster survivors. So far, $20 million is promised
articles.summary: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Villagers whose families prayed for generations at a local temple now gather around the mound of dirt where it once stood, unsure whether it will ever be rebuilt.
articles.body: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Villagers whose families prayed for generations at a local temple now gather around the mound of dirt where it once stood, unsure whether it will ever be rebuilt. Farmers who once grew rice to feed their families and earn a living now sit in makeshift shelters, wondering if they’ll ever own land again. In Nuwakot and surrounding areas of Nepal, where deadly floods in August washed away entire villages and left thousands dead or missing, life has ground to a halt. Along the Trishuli River, power lines, solar panels, cars and homes remain partially buried in the mud, while broken bridges leave communities cut off from neighboring towns. Survivors sleep in makeshift metal shelters, relying on donations for drinking water and food as they wait to see how, where and when they can get back on their feet. “God knows how long we will have to stay here,” 45-year-old Lakchin Bahadhur Tamang, a hydropower plant worker, told The Associated Press on a recent morning. “I fear that once these aid organizations and helping hands leave, we will be left helpless, without even enough drinking water.” Meanwhile, thousands of miles away at the U.N. climate summit in Turkey, known as COP31, leaders from Nepal and other mountain countries are warning the world there is no time to wait, as they sound the alarm about future disasters from global temperature rise, including the collapse of Himalayan glaciers. They and other climate activists are calling for discussions on the heightened peril that people face from a warming planet, caused mainly by the burning of gas, coal and oil. They are focusing in particular on a fund established three years ago to compensate developing nations hit hard by climate-fueled disasters. The fund doesn’t have nearly as much money as needed and is mired in bureaucracy. Experts say more funding and faster disbursement are essential to prepare for more efficient recovery as climate disasters become more frequent and severe. Nepal pushes for Himalayan climate resilience at COP31 Nepal and other mountain countries are pressing negotiators to make the dangers facing their communities a lasting priority. While Nepal and Bhutan sought a dedicated negotiating agenda item on warming in mountain regions at the start of the summit, their proposal did not make the cut. Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said the country wants a dedicated program on mountains and climate change so mountain risks are reflected in international climate action, including funding decisions. “After the disaster, we received an outpouring of sympathy. This is the time to put sympathy into the system,” Khanal said when speaking at the climate talks last week. The stakes extend far beyond mountain villages. Glaciers and snow in the Hindu Kush Himalaya feed rivers that nearly 2 billion people depend on for drinking water, farming and electricity, according to the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD. Warming can destabilize mountain slopes as glaciers retreat and frozen ground thaws. Floods carrying rock, ice and debris can cross borders within minutes, leaving little time to warn people downstream, especially as early warning systems face funding cuts. Temperature rise won’t stop any time soon Over the next years, global average temperatures are set to surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming compared to the early 1800s, a threshold that delegates set during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Amid that stark reality, many discussions focus on how and when the world can lower the global average temperature rise and go back below that threshold, which would require massive reductions in greenhouse gas emissions that the world has not been able to achieve. Pam Pearson, director of the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative, warned against treating the temperature rise as something that can be easily reversed. Snow and ice can disappear rapidly, while recovery can take centuries or millennia, she said. “There is no negotiating with the melting point of ice,” Pearson said. Monitoring unstable slopes and dangerous glacial lakes, sharing information across borders in real time, coordinating early warning systems and finding global funds are imperative, said climate experts at COP31. “Every time there’s a disaster in the Himalayas, we tend to call it a wake-up call,” said Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD. “The question before us is: What will it take for us to wake up and take action?” COP31 is a critical moment for the loss and damage fund The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage was established in 2022 to provide financial support to vulnerable developing nations suffering impacts from climate change. Its creation came after years of debates about how much developed nations, including the United States, historically the No. 1 polluter, should pay to help poorer nations adapt to climate change, which they had little role in causing. At COP31, one of the most constant refrains of protesters has been “climate justice now,” calling for help for Nepal. But the fund has so far fallen far short of expectations. For Nepal, it pledged about $20 million, only a fraction of the estimated $2.5 billion in losses. Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, has said rebuilding after the disaster would cost about one-tenth of Nepal’s economy. Manjeet Dhakal, a member of Nepal’s delegation and lead adviser to least developed countries at COP, welcomed the fund’s initial response but said that “the scale of the resources needs to increase.” Overall, experts have calculated that the amount currently pledged through the fund falls vastly short of the world’s future needs. Countries have pledged more than $820 million to the fund, while it faces 176 requests for support from developing nations totaling about $2.8 billion. The fund’s board members will meet in December to consider more support requests. The Stockholm Environment Institute estimated that by 2030 the loss and damage finance needed in lower-income countries would be between $400 billion and $1.6 trillion per year. The loss and damage fund has been slow to turn promises into payouts. Money earmarked for Nepal remains subject to a formal funding proposal and final board approval, with no disbursement date announced. For survivors in Nepal, the gap between what has been offered and what is needed is huge. Standing between destroyed buildings, 41-year-old Dhurba Bhandari, a small store owner, noted that his country had contributed very little to global carbon emissions yet had been devastated. “The international community must take responsibility and help people who have been displaced, as well as support reconstruction,” he said.

articles.title: Leonid meteor shower 2026: When and where to see it from where you live
articles.summary: The Leonids, among the year’s fastest meteor showers, peak on November 17-18. Find the best time to watch in your city.
articles.body:
Some of the fastest meteors in the night sky return this week, as the Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night between November 17 and 18.

Racing at about 71km (44 miles) per second, they burn up as bright streaks, sometimes leaving glowing trails that hang in the sky for seconds.

In this visual explainer, see how the shower forms as Earth crosses a comet’s dust trail, then search for your city to find the best viewing time.

A meteor shower happens when dozens, or sometimes hundreds, of “shooting stars” streak across the night sky. In reality, they are not stars, but tiny bits of space debris burning up in Earth’s atmosphere.

Most of this debris comes from comets, which are icy bodies that orbit the sun and shed dust as they get closer to it. When Earth’s orbit crosses one of these dust trails, the particles, called meteoroids, hit the atmosphere at high speed and heat up. They glow as meteors and usually burn up long before reaching the ground.

The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, whose dust trail Earth passes through every November. Drag the slider below to follow Earth through 2026 and see when it meets the stream.

What makes the Leonid meteor shower special?

The Leonids are named after the constellation Leo, the point in the sky from which they appear to come. They are known for fireballs, which are unusually bright meteors from larger bits of debris. They also produce Earth-grazers, meteors that skim the upper atmosphere at a shallow angle and leave long trails near the horizon.

What really sets them apart is their storms. Comet Tempel-Tuttle passes close to the sun about every 33 years and leaves debris behind. When that happens, the shower can produce a storm of at least 1,000 meteors an hour.

The 1833 storm over North America helped scientists work out where meteors come from. In 1966, thousands of meteors fell every minute for about 15 minutes. The most recent storms came in 1999, 2001 and 2002, and the comet next swings close to the sun in 2031.

The Leonids can appear in any part of the sky, so the best approach is to find a dark spot with a wide view, lie back and take in as much sky as you can.

If you trace their paths backwards, the meteors all seem to streak out from a single point known as the radiant. This is an effect of perspective: the debris travels along roughly parallel paths, but the meteors appear to spread out from one point, much like railway tracks seem to meet in the distance.

For the Leonids, the radiant lies in the constellation Leo, which rises in the east around midnight.

When and how to watch from where you live

According to the International Meteor Organization (IMO), the Leonids are active from November 6 to 30 and are expected to peak on the night between November 17 and 18, around 23:45 GMT on Tuesday. Under clear, dark skies, the IMO expects up to about 15 meteors an hour at the peak.

The best time to watch is between midnight and dawn, as Leo climbs higher in the sky. The moon, which will be about half full on the peak night, sets around midnight in many places, leaving darker skies for the rest of the night.

Find a spot away from city lights and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the dark.

Use the widget below to find the best viewing times in your city.

Can you see the Leonid meteor shower from both hemispheres?

Yes. The Leonids are visible from the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere, but conditions are generally better in the north, where Leo climbs higher in the sky. South of the equator, the best chance is in the hour or two before dawn.

Will the moon affect the Leonid meteor shower in 2026?

Only slightly. The moon reaches its first quarter on November 17 and sets around midnight, so it should not interfere much during the best viewing hours.

How do the Leonids compare with other meteor showers?

The Leonids are far from the busiest shower. Under ideal conditions, the IMO puts their peak rate at about 15 meteors an hour, compared with about 100 for the Perseids in August and about 150 for the Geminids in December. What they lack in numbers, they make up for in speed and their history of storms.

articles.title: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
articles.summary: The ongoing Israeli assault continues to have disastrous consequences for the people of southern Lebanon.
articles.body:
Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children.

Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors.

Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible.

Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words.

Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera.

“What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.”

More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations.

Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023.

We have repeatedly filmed children’s clothes, toys and school books among the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes, and repeatedly attended funerals of children killed alongside their parents. It is just as difficult emotionally to talk to survivors who show signs of trauma and tell us they live in fear.

In the village of Tibnine, close to the northern edge of the area occupied by the Israeli army, 11-year-old Bannine took us to the second floor of an orphanage, to show us what a nearby Israeli air strike did to their rooms.

“We were not here when this happened,” Bannine told us in a room full of debris and broken glass. Stuffed animals and clothes were still scattered on the floor.

Hundreds of thousands of people returned to their villages in southern Lebanon because of a reduction in violence in recent months. But there is little sense of security, with Israeli strikes and home demolitions continuing in front line areas.

“We wake up and sleep to the sound of bombing and warplanes and irritating drones,” Anaya Sultan told us. Her father was killed when the Israeli military escalated the conflict earlier this year. “He was my soul … he was everything to me,” she added.

Some of the girls here are not orphans, but their parents are too poor to care for them. According to Lebanese officials, the region’s economy is in a state of collapse.

Recurring conflicts, ruined infrastructure, blocked access to agricultural land, and mass displacement are making it hard for families in southern Lebanon to sustain themselves.

The UN identified southern Lebanon – alongside impoverished northern and eastern regions such as Akkar and Baalbek – as areas of greatest concern where families are struggling to survive.

According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than 1 million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity.

“Unfortunately, so many people are displaced … many of them used to support and help us. They are not present and they themselves are struggling,” Bassima Fawaz, who helps manage the orphanage, told us as we walked through the cold hallways and rooms of the building.

“We had to cover the windows with plastic sheeting because there’s no money to replace the glass shattered by Israeli bombardment. One of our girls is in hospital with pneumonia.”

articles.title: Duffy vows to modernize aging air traffic system after nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says Friday's FAA ground stop was no hack, as the FAA probes a router issue, network problem or installation error.
articles.body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday said he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America" following a nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded more than a million passengers. During an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," Duffy said he wants to build a modern, resilient telecommunications network. "Congress did give me $12.5 billion. That’s for radar and radios. I am well on my way to deploying all that money. You can’t buy this off the shelf, so I’ve ordered it. As it is delivered, we pay for it, and we deploy it into the NAS. But what’s really important is the next phase of the investment," he told host Sean Hannity on Monday. The $12.5 billion in congressional funding is part of a broader effort to modernize the nation's air traffic control system, including communications, surveillance and other infrastructure. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' "So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network. You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America," he continued. Duffy added that the department needs new software. "The software we use to manage our airplanes in the airspace was built in the 1990s. It works. It works well. But if we’re going to drive more safety and more efficiency, we need brand-new software," he explained. The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence that a cyberattack forced the ground stop on Friday and that the Federal Aviation Administration was investigating whether a network problem, router issue or installation error caused the system failure. The FAA is working with contractor L3Harris, which installed the router in question and is assisting with the investigation at its Florida laboratory. "We had all of our intelligence agencies, at Donald Trump’s direction, talk on Friday night," Duffy said. "No one was seeing any kind of hack into our system. And we’ve now secured the router." BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We’re doing an analysis in Florida with L3Harris and the FAA. I actually asked the FBI to come in just to make sure, to put people at ease, that this was not a hack. So I think it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error," he continued. The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.

articles.summary: A cat that went missing after a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn last week has been found alive and reunited with his 13-year-old owner, New York City
articles.body: A cat that went missing after a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn last week has been found alive and reunited with his 13-year-old owner, New York City officials said on Sunday.Isaac was discovered inside the apartment of Zariah Coleman, who lives in a building next to the one that collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood.Rescue workers found him inside a cabinet under the kitchen sink after hearing a faint meow, according to a report by The New York Times.Coleman and her family had not been allowed to return to their apartment since Wednesday's collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced residents of nearby buildings to evacuate. The collapse also tore away part of the side of their building, leaving a hole where Coleman's bedroom wall had been.Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor's Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with his owner.Coleman waited outside as workers brought the cat out of the building. She hugged his carrier as he was rescued, having survived four days without food or water. Isaac was then taken to Flatbush Cats' veterinary clinic for a medical check-up.“I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Coleman told The New York Times. “I knew they would.”Girl had appealed for help to find missing catColeman had made an emotional appeal at a news conference on Friday, asking rescuers to continue searching for her pet.“I just really hope they come and get our cat. He's hiding from them, and I think he's scared,” she had told reporters.In comments to the Daily Mail, Coleman recalled that her immediate concern after the collapse was Isaac. “The first thing I thought about was my cat,” she said.She had wanted to search for him but was worried about what she might encounter amid the devastation. “I realized I didn’t know what I was gonna face,” she said.Flatbush Cats executive director Will Zweigart entered the building, working in coordination with the city's Department of Buildings, to rescue Isaac from the family's apartment.The cat is receiving veterinary care following his rescue. The Daily Mail reported that doctors hoped he could be released to his family within a few days.Mayor thanks rescue teams for reunionNew York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani welcomed the news of Isaac's rescue in a social media post on Sunday, thanking Taylor's office, the Department of Buildings and Flatbush Cats for their work.“Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We're grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”The collapse on November 11 killed eight people and injured 18 others, including four firefighters and 14 civilians. The disaster also forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, leaving residents unable to return to their homes.The cause of the collapse remains under investigation. The Daily Mail reported that authorities were examining excavation work at an adjoining construction site, while the Brooklyn district attorney's office had also opened a criminal investigation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.

BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.

Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.

Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.

Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.

Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.

His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

articles.title: A safe containing $55,737 was discovered behind a fire station in Falmouth, Maine, in August 2022; after four years without an owner coming forward, the money is being redirected to help families pay heating bills
articles.summary: A safe discovered on a wooded trail behind a fire station in Maine contained a mystery that investigators could not solve for four years: $55,737 in cash,
articles.body: A safe discovered on a wooded trail behind a fire station in Maine contained a mystery that investigators could not solve for four years: $55,737 in cash, with no clear explanation of who had left it there or why. Despite contacting other law enforcement agencies, tracing the money and publicising the discovery, police never found its owner. Now, the unexplained stash is set to serve a very different purpose. According to The Portland Press Herald, the town of Falmouth is redirecting the money towards heating assistance for residents struggling to afford their winter energy bills.The discovery dates back to August 2022, when a local resident walking along a wooded trail came across a safe near Falmouth's Central Fire Station and nearby baseball fields. The resident alerted authorities, and police took possession of the safe. When officers opened it, they found $55,737 in cash.The unusual discovery immediately raised questions. Who had put such a large amount of money inside a safe and left it in the woods? Had it been abandoned, misplaced or intended for someone to collect? There was no obvious way to establish its owner or explain how it had ended up behind the fire station.Falmouth Police Chief John Kilbride and his department began trying to trace its origins. Investigators contacted law enforcement agencies in Maine and neighbouring New Hampshire, hoping someone might recognise the circumstances surrounding the cash. They also followed the money to a bank in New Hampshire, which confirmed that it had not been reported as stolen. Police went through the required procedures for unclaimed property, including publicising that a substantial sum of money had been found. Notices were intended to give anyone who had lost the cash an opportunity to come forward and establish a legitimate claim.But no one did. The mystery remained unresolved even after months of investigation. According to the police department, there were no credible leads identifying the owner or explaining why the safe had been left in the woods. Kilbride told local media that investigators had considered several possibilities, including whether the money was meant to be collected as part of an exchange. However, he acknowledged that this was speculation and that police did not know what had actually happened.The chief also wanted to ensure that enough time was given for a possible owner to discover the loss. The money was not immediately treated as a windfall for the town. Instead, it remained under police control while officials waited for someone to claim it. After four years without anyone coming forward, the unclaimed cash was eventually set to be put to public use. Under Maine's rules governing unclaimed property, the money had to be directed towards a charitable purpose rather than simply becoming an unrestricted source of municipal funds.That opened the door to a proposal that could benefit residents as winter approaches. Falmouth Town Manager Nathan Poore suggested using the money for heating assistance, an issue that can become particularly pressing in Maine, where cold winters make heating a significant household expense. The Falmouth Town Council subsequently voted to direct the funds towards the town's low-income home energy assistance programme, known as LIHEAP. The decision means that money which had remained locked away in an unexplained safe could help households pay for essential heating during the colder months.The funds are expected to become available to eligible residents from January 2027. The proposal discussed by town officials included assistance of around $500 per applicant, with approximately 50 households expected to benefit based on previous programme demand. The precise distribution will depend on the town's implementation and eligibility process.Council Chair Bryce Hach described the discovery as an unusual source of funding, emphasising that the money had not come from taxpayers or from a planned municipal policy. In comments reported by WGME, he called it a gift that had effectively fallen into the community's lap. He also pointed to the timing of the decision. With the heating season approaching and fuel costs placing pressure on household budgets, the council believed the money could provide meaningful relief to residents who needed help keeping their homes warm.The assistance will be particularly relevant in a state where heating is not a minor seasonal expense. Maine has a large number of households that rely on heating oil, making fluctuations in fuel prices a significant concern for families, older residents and people living on limited incomes. For households already balancing rent, groceries, electricity and other bills, the cost of keeping a home warm can become difficult to manage during a prolonged winter.Maine already has state and federally supported programmes designed to help low-income households with energy expenses. LIHEAP, for instance, provides assistance to eligible residents with heating costs. articles.title: How moves to 'de-pave' Oswestry could cut flash floods
articles.summary: Work is being done around Oswestry to use natural solutions to help combat the effects of flooding.
articles.body:
More than £380,000 is being spent in Oswestry to help reduce the effects of flash flooding.

Rather than flood defences, it will focus on natural measures designed to "de-pave" the north Shropshire town and help water soak into the ground more easily.

The project is one of eight being supported through the Severn Valley Water Management Scheme, which is run by the Environment Agency, Shropshire Council and a number of bodies in Wales.

In this case, raised flower beds will be built alongside rain gardens - shallow, planted areas that are designed to capture, hold, and naturally absorb water run-off.

The Senior Citizens Hub on Lorne Street, and the town's central car park are among the areas identified.

The wider Severn Valley Water Management Scheme is using a variety of measures to reduce the risk of flooding on the upper stretches of the River Severn.

Pete Lambert, from the Environment Agency, said: "There's two ways the scheme is going to approach it - firstly in temporary flood storage, so engineering, that's our traditional approach to managing water.

"But then the second approach is to look at the whole two-and-a-half thousand square kilometres [of landscape] and say how we adapt land management, so that the water slows itself down."

Volunteers at Oswestry's Senior Citizens Club said the building's car park could be challenging to use because of groundwater.

A team from Shropshire Wildlife Trust has helped design a space that could help stop this from happening.

Chloe French, from the organisation, said she hopes by using both native and drought tolerant plants, it could tackle problems the building on Lorne Street faces.

"The aim in this area is a rain garden. We are also augmenting the drainage that the site currently has itself to help feed it all together to link up the connectivity," French said.

"We are harvesting rainwater from the roof and from the gutters and using that to help keep the plants that we'll be putting in vibrant."

The central car park is also expected to get a rain garden before Christmas.

"We also have a preschool that we're working with to introduce permeable paving and a living wall and activities that children can take ownership of to grow their own plants and climbers," French added.
