articles.title: So You Are: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
articles.summary: The remains of a top Australian racehorse that died of colic on Monday were found at a public rubbish tip.
articles.body:
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.

In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.

Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".

Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.

The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.

"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.

Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.

In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.

"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."

"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."

The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.

"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."

Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.

The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

articles.title: Bahrain thwarts drone attack; Iran claims targeting US radar
articles.summary: The IRGC says the attack is part of efforts to counter ‘hostile activities of US forces in the region’.
articles.body:
Bahraini air defence has thwarted a drone attack, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a barrage of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

The IRGC said on Tuesday the “precision operation” targeted a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain. The attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, it added, according to a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB.

In a statement later on Tuesday, the US military said the attack drones “were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel”.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital, Manama, after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Ministry of Interior’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It later issued an “all clear” message.

In a statement, the ministry said “precautionary measures remain in place” and urged the public to exercise caution.

The attacks in Bahrain – home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has affected the entire Gulf region and beyond.

Also on Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry denied a CNN report quoting unnamed sources that it potentially planned to detonate “a dirty bomb” in Washington, DC. The ministry’s spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on X that the allegations were “baseless”.

In recent days, Iran has claimed attacks on US radar systems Bahrain.

On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa airbase, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions.

On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or casualties.

“Since Friday, it seems that the rules of engagement have changed,” said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, stating that a pattern has emerged, with Iran now trying to restore deterrence.

“First, Iran warned that if the US escorts ships carrying oil that do not coordinate with Iran [through the Strait of Hormuz], then Tehran would attack US military installations. Now, Iran is saying its attack on a US radar system in Bahrain is because of the US’s continued violations of Iranian airspace.

It is not a response to a specific US attack, but rather the continued violation of its airspace.”

Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

articles.title: Ukraine strike collapses section of Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea
articles.summary: A section of a strategic bridge connecting Russia and occupied Crimea has collapsed after a Ukrainian strike. Meanwhile, much of Kyiv was brought to a standstill after Moscow hit two of its key bridges overnight.
articles.body: A section of a multi-billion dollar strategic bridge connecting Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula has collapsed following a Ukrainian strike. Meanwhile, much of Kyiv was brought to a standstill on Tuesday after Moscow hit two of its key bridges overnight. The Crimean Bridge, also known as the Kerch Bridge, is a vital supply line for Moscow’s troops and has huge symbolic value for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who made its construction a key priority after Russia’s illegal annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula in 2014. Ukraine has stepped up its attacks against Crimea in the past six months, forcing the Russian-installed authorities to impose a state of emergency over the summer because of widespread power outages and fuel shortages on the heavily militarized peninsula. The timing of the latest attack, on the eve of Putin’s meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia, makes it even more symbolic. The Kremlin has sought to frame the gathering as a “New Yalta” in a nod to the 1945 conference at which Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively redrew the global map of spheres of influence with the Allied powers. The attack on the bridge makes Yalta, a city in annexed Crimea, effectively inaccessible from mainland Russia, at least until it is repaired. “It is of fundamental importance: The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – using our technologies and our solutions,” Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also confirmed Tuesday that domestically manufactured missiles and drones were used in the attack, including Neptune missiles that he said struck the railway section of the bridge and Palianytsia drones that targeted the road section. “Today, at the key stage, the ‘Palianytsia’ drones performed exceptionally well, striking the road section of the bridge, while ‘Neptune’ missiles, ‘Ruta’ drones, and FP-5 drones struck the railway section,” Zelensky said in a statement posted on X. Zelensky said the strike was the seventh stage of what he called “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.” “As a result of the strikes, one of the metal arches and the road span beneath it were completely destroyed,” said Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, adding that the railway section of the bridge was also “preliminarily damaged.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov sought to play down the impact of the attack, saying the bridge would be rebuilt “even better than before,” according to Russian state news agency TASS, citing the Izvestia newspaper. Traffic suspended The $3.7 billion bridge, which at nearly 12 miles is the longest crossing in Europe, was built to handle 40,000 cars a day and move 14 million passengers and 13 million tons of cargo per year, according to Russian state media. Videos and images geolocated by CNN appear to show a portion of the road bridge collapsed into the water. The parallel rail bridge appeared still to be standing. In another video geolocated by CNN, a fire can be seen burning on a section of the bridge. Traffic has been suspended following the second Ukrainian attack in as many days, Russia’s transport ministry said, adding that the bridge was damaged in a drone attack. “Experts are assessing the damage,” said the ministry, adding that there were no casualties. Railway traffic across the bridge has since resumed, according to TASS. Moscow-backed Crimea governor Sergei Aksyonov said passengers without vehicles could also use a ferry crossing. Russia’s Investigative Committee confirmed the attack on the bridge, calling it a “terrorist act by Ukrainian armed groups.” Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the Kerch Bridge since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, but the damage the bridge sustained this week appears to be more significant than in some of the previous attacks. Russia’s military said its air defenses had shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight. Key bridges in Kyiv attacked The Ukrainian capital Kyiv also came under intense bombardment overnight into Tuesday. Two people were killed and the city’s North and South bridges badly damaged in the assault, officials said. “Last night, four ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge and three struck the Northern Bridge,” Zelensky said in a separate statement on X. Kyiv is split in half by the Dnipro River. The right bank is home to the majority of the city’s business centers, offices and government institutions, while the left bank is mostly residential. The bridges connecting the two sides are crucial – some 600,000 vehicles as well as trains and Kyiv’s metro cross them every day. “Critical infrastructure systems have been damaged, causing disruptions to water and heat supply in some districts,” the city office said. Zelensky also confirmed “significant” power outages in the Dnipro, Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia regions, saying emergency and repair crews were working to deal with the consequences of the Russian strike on the power grid. The attacks on the bridges have led to major traffic jams on both the left and right banks, although the scale of damage was still being clarified, officials said. Russia’s military said it had targeted Ukrainian military, transportation, energy and port infrastructure, using drones and ground- and air-based precision-guided weapons. Trump-Xi-Putin to talk Ukraine The exchange of attacks on critical infrastructure come two days before the planned trilateral talks between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit. Trump said Monday he expects to discuss the war in Ukraine with his Russian and Chinese counterparts, despite US officials suggesting last week the topic wouldn’t be on the table. “We’ll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House. “Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” he said, without giving any source for that claim. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said last week that Russia was losing “more than 40,000 troops – killed or seriously wounded – every month.” Peskov said the recent attacks by Kyiv could be linked to the upcoming trilateral meeting, according to Russian state media outlet Vesti, but provided no evidence to support the claim. In October, Zelensky voiced concern that a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin might lead to dealmaking about the future of Ukraine without Kyiv being consulted.

articles.title: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in Canada luxury car theft syndicate
articles.summary: Canadian authorities say they have recovered 96 luxury vehicles destined for West Africa.
articles.body:
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.

They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.

Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.

The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.

The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.

The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".

The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.

Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.

"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.

Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.

Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.

"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.

Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.

In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.

They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

articles.title: Ukraine drone attack kills two in Crimea as Kyiv targets bridge to Russia
articles.summary: Moscow-installed governor says traffic suspended after second attack on bridge in two days.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive day, according to the Moscow-installed governor.

In a Telegram post, Sergei Aksyonov said traffic has been suspended after Tuesday’s attack on the Kerch Bridge .

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the “unprecedented” attack, publishing footage on social media on Tuesday that showed the main arch of the bridge for cars and part of its roadway collapsed.

He said the targeting came in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure.

The bridge in the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, stretches for 19km (11.8 miles) and is also used by trains.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said Russia came under one of the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Monday night.

“According to official data from the Ministry of Defence, Russian air defence systems destroyed more than 1,400 drones over 23 regions, including border regions and regions in central Russia. Meanwhile, the mayor of Moscow said that more than 800 drones flew towards the capital,” Shapovalova reported.

Also on Tuesday, Moscow attacked two bridges in Kyiv, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a Telegram post that ⁠the Northern and ⁠Southern bridges had been hit and the subway ⁠system ⁠had also been damaged. He added that water and power supplies had been ‌partially cut.

The Russian Defence Ministry said it also targeted Ukraine’s military infrastructure in attacks on Monday night, including facilities used to produce cruise missiles and long‑ and medium‑range drones. The ministry said transport and energy facilities were also targeted as well as port infrastructure and ships used by the Ukrainian military.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the first of a “series of very loud explosions” rang out in Kyiv just before midnight.

“Another round of explosions was heard just after 5am [03:00 GMT] this morning,” she said.

“Some bridges were damaged. We understand that they are still standing, but there is no traffic on either of them. These are bridges that are used every day by civilians to commute around the city. These attacks also cut heating to hundreds of apartment buildings on Kyiv’s Left Bank.”

The exchange of attacks comes just days before a meeting of Presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia, Xi Jinping of China and Donald Trump of the United States in China’s Shenzhen region.

The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Thursday’s talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.

Trump has made securing an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine a key part of his presidency. Despite another round of talks held in the United Arab Emirates last week, US mediators have failed to make a breakthrough.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Kyiv would carry out attacks on Russia in the days before the meeting.

articles.title: ‘I tell it like it is’: Pope Leo talks cancer diagnosis, married priests and being hit in the face with a rosary
articles.summary: Pope Leo said his faith in democracy is what makes him an American, as he gave wide-ranging remarks that touched on his cancer diagnosis, church doctrine and the question of married priests on board the papal plane back to Rome from his visit to South America.
articles.body: Pope Leo said his faith in democracy is what makes him an American, as he gave wide-ranging remarks that touched on his cancer diagnosis, church doctrine and the question of married priests on board the papal plane back to Rome from his visit to South America. The pope, who also holds Peruvian citizenship, explained that “in many ways” he’s a “gringo, an American,” and this is apparent through his belief in democracy and how he addressed his recent surgery and health difficulties. “When I talk about things, I’m generally straightforward, I tell it like it is,” he told reporters during an in-flight news conference on the plane departing from Lima. “When it comes to my health – even talking about it, like saying ‘well I’m going through this’ – that wouldn’t be typical in many countries and in many cultures, but in the United States it’s a bit more common.” He added, “My deep faith in democracy and democratic participation is also part of being American.” On his flight out to South America, the first US-born pope told CNN that he was “proud to be an American” and had cast a mail-in ballot during the US midterm election, likely the first time a pope has voted in secular, democratic elections. On board the plane home after his trip, the pope addressed his health saying he is still “not 100%” but feels “quite well” and that “endurance is one of the gifts the Lord has given me.” The pope explained that the discovery of a growth on his lung came as a “surprise” during a routine annual check-up, and that he had not experienced any symptoms before the tests. His surgery on October 13 removed the lower lobe of his right lung, and since then the pope has made a good recovery. Leo stressed, however, that he didn’t see the need to sign a letter of resignation should he become incapacitated or fall into a coma, as some of his predecessors had done, explaining that church law makes provisions for such a scenario but that he would consider it in the future. During the 45-minute news conference, he covered a range of topics including the question of married priests in the Catholic Church, pertinent given he had visited the Amazon region of Peru where there is a drastic shortage of clergy. A major church gathering convened by Pope Francis in 2019 had petitioned to allow for the ordination of married men in the Amazon. The pope said he would not make any changes in the short term to maintain church unity, but it was a topic that remained under discussion. “It’s not the only solution, but it’s a solution, which in certain areas of the church can cause division because there is not universal… acceptance of that concept,” he said, adding that his priority had been to promote unity. “The Pope doesn’t change church doctrine,” he added. “We all have to listen. The bishops have to listen. It may be in the future that some things will change.” But he stressed that an “important part of my ministry to the church is to heal, bring people together,” and to “consider what we believe the priorities need to be, and then we’ll see how we walk forward from there.” The Roman Catholic Church made celibacy a mandatory requirement for ordination to the priesthood in the 12th century, although there are exceptions. Leo XIV said his meeting with victims of abuse within the church in Peru (he also met survivors in Argentina), was aimed at helping victims find a path that can gradually “lead them toward genuine healing” while representing a commitment that such abuses “never happen again.” He added that the Vatican was studying the topic of “spiritual abuse” within the church and trying to give it a legal definition, even though it remains a “vague concept.” Although President Javier Milei’s austerity measures and funding cuts have affected the Catholic Church’s charitable work in Argentina, Pope Leo said his encounter with the Argentinian president had been “a positive encounter” and that they had been able to find a shared understanding on “the value of life – the value of the human being at every stage.” Milei, who was seen in tears saying goodbye to Leo as he left Argentina, “showed an openness to hear this message,” the pope said. Leo also saw the funny side of being hit on the face with a religious item during the final mass in Lima. He said it was simply someone “of great faith” who wanted to offer him a rosary and showed the enthusiasm and deep faith in Peru. “These are things that one carries in the heart, perhaps in your eye,” he added. Finally, the pope said he was not planning to ease restrictions on the traditional Latin Mass, which was codified in the 16th century and then reformed following a gathering of bishops at the Second Vatican Council, 1962-65. While Leo pointed out that the older liturgy can be celebrated with a dispensation, some have been pushing him to ease restrictions put in place by his predecessor, who said he had become concerned about some Catholics using the older liturgy to undermine church unity. The traditional Latin Mass has several high-profile supporters including Shia LaBeouf, the actor, and Harrison Butker, the Kansas City Chiefs kicker.

articles.title: Handwritten draft of MLK’s ‘I Have a Dream’ speech on display before being auctioned
articles.summary: Words scrawled in blue pen — and others scratched out — give an intimate peek into the writing of what would become the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s most famous speech.
articles.body: ATLANTA — Words scrawled in blue pen — and others scratched out — give an intimate peek into the writing of what would become the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s most famous speech. Delivered Aug. 28, 1963, from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, the “I Have a Dream” speech reflects on the shameful legacy of slavery, segregation and discrimination and looks forward with hope to future equality for the country’s Black citizens. A handwritten draft of that speech goes on display in King’s hometown this week before it is sold to the highest bidder at auction in January. “It shows a genius at work, that these words didn’t just spill out perfectly,” said Jill Savitt, president and CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, where the draft is on display through Sunday. The speech that was delivered at the March on Washington The words that became most famous do not appear in the draft. The “I have a dream” refrain was added by King as he stood before a crowd of tens of thousands of people gathered on the National Mall for the March on Washington. Watching footage from the speech that day, it is “almost like an electric charge goes through him and he is overcome and he goes on the riff about ‘I have a dream’ — that was ad-libbed from the stage,” Savitt said. Other key parts of the speech, titled “Normalcy — Never Again,” are there in the civil rights icon’s own handwriting, including the opening lines and the powerful finish invoking an African American spiritual. The seven pages from a pad of yellow, lined paper are displayed in two cases in the Atlanta museum’s gallery devoted to the March on Washington. Video of King delivering the speech is projected on the wall behind them. King completed the handwritten draft in his hotel room in the wee hours of the morning, less than 12 hours before it was delivered, according to Christie’s, which will handle the sale of the manuscript. It was then given to assistants to be typed and sent to the media. Peter Klarnet, a specialist in books and manuscripts at Christie’s, said he was “just blown away” when he first saw the draft, which is so close to the final typed version that it must be the final handwritten draft, he said. “It’s such an important piece of American history and it’s a part of world history,” Klarnet said. “This is a speech that inspired all of us to do better.” How the draft surfaced six decades later Speechwriter Edward Clayton was among the multiple advisers who helped King hash out the content of the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, who worked alongside him in the civil rights movement, discovered the draft in the late 1990s, three decades after her husband’s death. It was in a drawer of his desk, tucked inside an envelope labeled “speech.” “The two of them gelled with writing and words,” Xernona Clayton said in a Christie’s news release. “They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time.” Clayton knew the document was important but didn’t realize it was the only remaining handwritten draft and stuck it back in the drawer, finding it there again just two years ago. What’s next for the speech draft Clayton, who established the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust to advance causes important to her, decided after consultation with trusted advisers to sell the draft to support charities that advance her own legacy and that of King. Christie’s expects the draft to fetch more than $10 million. The organizations that will benefit include the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta. “I am so grateful for the opportunity to give this amazing speech new life, and to give new life to people who are in need,” Clayton said. “And we cannot wait to give that first gift.” King’s two remaining living children, the Rev. Bernice King and Martin Luther King III, said in the Christie’s release that they are grateful the sale will support the legacy of the movement their father helped build. “It is poetic that the past will protect the future,” Martin Luther King III said. “We are grateful that this treasure was preserved over decades by the Clayton family. It is a remarkable piece of history that shines a light on our father’s process as he prepared to make a speech that so profoundly affected the course of the Civil Rights movement and our nation. Now, for the first time, the public will have the opportunity to be inspired by this document.” The draft is being publicly displayed for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from Monday through Sunday. It will be shown at Christie’s in New York from Jan. 15, King’s birthday, through Jan. 21 before being offered for auction on Jan. 22. Klarnet said they are also trying to arrange additional showings of the draft before the sale.

articles.title: L’Oreal U.S. settles hair relaxer cancer cases during first trial
articles.summary: Four women who said they were diagnosed with cancer as a result of chemical hair straightening products reached a settlement on Monday with ​L’Oreal’s subsidiary and other companies during a trial in Chicago.
articles.body: CHICAGO, Nov 16 — Four women who said they were diagnosed with cancer as a result of chemical hair straightening products reached a settlement on Monday with ​L’Oreal’s subsidiary and other companies during a trial in Chicago, according to ‌their attorneys. The women are among thousands who have sued the companies, alleging that years of using chemical hair straighteners caused them to develop gynecologic cancers. The cases, which were the first to go to trial, ​settled for a confidential sum, the lawyers said. A spokesperson for L’Oreal said the ​company’s highest priority is the health and wellbeing of its consumers, and ⁠it remains confident in the safety of its SoftSheen-Carson brand hair products, which include ​hair relaxers. “L’Oréal USA strictly follows all regulations in every market in which it operates, and ​its products are always subject to a rigorous scientific evaluation of their safety,” the spokesperson said. In a statement, Danielle Ward Mason, an attorney for the women, MaryAnne Lindsey, Surenthia Jenkins, Miranda Lofton and Sandra ​Simpson, said she hoped the settlement would give the women a sense of justice. The women ​sued L’Oreal’s U.S. subsidiary and several other makers of the products in Cook County, Illinois, in 2023 ‌and ⁠2024. The trial began on November 9 with jury selection. While some cases have been filed in state court, more than 12,700 cases over the claims are centralized before a judge in federal court in Chicago, court records show. The products, which have been marketed under the ​names Dark and Lovely, ​Optimum and other ⁠brands, promise to permanently straighten textured hair and have been widely marketed to Black women. The first lawsuits hit the docket after the ​2022 release of a study done by the National Institutes of ​Health that found ⁠women who used the products several times a year were more than twice as likely to develop uterine cancer. L’Oreal has said the study did not establish a causal link between the ⁠use ​of the products and any conditions alleged by the ​plaintiffs. At least two states, Arizona and Minnesota, sued L’Oreal over the products this year, alleging that the company had misled ​women about their safety.

articles.title: New York Mayor Mamdani disbands divisive NYPD unit
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the police department’s Strategic Response Group, a specialized unit critics say is too militaristic when it comes to handling mass protests.
articles.body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the police department’s Strategic Response Group, a specialized unit critics say is too militaristic when it comes to handling mass protests, but one others argue is essential to counter-terrorism operations. Mamdani has repeatedly said he doesn’t believe terrorism duties and responses to First Amendment-related incidents should fall under one unit, and he made disbanding the unit a key pledge of his 2025 mayoral campaign. Under the plan rolled out Monday, those two priorities — counter-terror and protest-related duties — will be decoupled. Counter-terror duties move under the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau. Starting in the new year, the city will restructure its response to protests through the creation of a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). That group, created within the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety, will not have weapons or arrest powers, Mamdani said in Monday’s announcement. “New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation,” Mamdani said in a statement. The mayor said it was part of “building a new approach to public safety.” To support that civilian-led group, the NYPD is creating a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) made of 30 officers trained in communication and de-escalation. FAST will lead those efforts until the new civilian-led team is established. The reforms put forward Monday by the mayor and police commissioner also address restrictions on police tactics during First Amendment activities. Mamdani says officers will not be allowed to use pepper spray as a crowd-management tool and long-range acoustic devices must stay below 90 decibels. “Today, we announced a new structure designed to consolidate our counterterrorism capabilities, provide greater support to our patrol officers and ensure we continue to respond to protests consistent with public safety and the First Amendment,” Tisch said. “I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat. These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department,” the statement from the commissioner read. According to the NYPD, the SRG “responds to citywide mobilizations, civil disorders, and major events with highly trained personnel and specialized equipment. They are also deployed to areas requiring an increased police presence due to increased crime or other conditions.” The SRG has been a polarizing entity within the city’s police force, facing accusations of being too violent and too militaristic, especially when it comes to crowd control during protests. In 2020, they were accused of unlawfully detaining over 100 demonstrators during the George Floyd protests. Three years later, a legal settlement was announced in 2023, in part as reparations tied to these detentions. That settlement now governs how and when the NYPD deploys the SRG, though Mamdani has given Tisch significant latitude when it comes to those operations. Also that year, the City Council’s Public Safety Committee held a hearing about the Strategic Response Group. Unit representatives didn’t attend “due to ongoing litigation,” the NYPD said at the time. It submitted written testimony instead that said, in part, that the “SRG is comprised of highly trained, well-vetted and professional police officers.” “These officers are called upon in some of the most stressful, dangerous and chaotic situations, such as the protests and riots that occurred during the summer of 2020,” that written testimony statement said. The approximately 600 officers who were part of the SRG will reassigned when the group is dissolved, which according to the mayor’s order, will happen by mid-February. The move has already triggered backlash from police unions. “Why change it? It doesn’t need to be changed. It’s working. It’s working,” said Detectives Endowment Association President Scott Munro. But advocates say the mayor made the right move. “Good news for New Yorkers. Good news for public safety. Good news for the first amendment,” said Donna Lieberman, of the New York Civil Liberties Union. “The numbers of civilian, of CCRB complaints against members of this unit were off the wall compared to the rest of the entire police department.” When asked about the issue on Friday, Mamdani said there would “absolutely” be no reduction in police response time to mass incidents. “I have been very clear the focus of the conversations since being in office has been how to do this in a way that keeps New Yorkers safe and protects their First Amendment rights,” the mayor added.

images.caption: Officers with the NYPD's Strategic Response Group break up a student-led protest against the ongoing war in Gaza at Brooklyn College in 2025.

articles.title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest Pearl Harbor survivor, dies at 106
articles.summary: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died.
articles.body: BOSTON — Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died. Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson. “It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” said Diane Johnson, 72. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.” Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn’t hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane. “While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship. Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea. “We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn’t see any land at all. All you saw was ocean,” he said. “I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don’t tell you anything if you don’t need to know. And I didn’t need to know it. So they tell you nothing.” The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105. While Johnson didn’t see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II. He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship’s preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea. Johnson also witnessed the war’s end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa’s mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945. “I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table,” he said. “It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let’s go home.” For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn’t see it as one of the defining moments in his life. Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90. “Pearl Harbor just happened. I can’t put it any other way,” he said.

articles.title: Van Gogh auction to go ahead, despite last-minute claim the $180M painting was sold ‘under duress’ in Nazi era
articles.summary: Sotheby’s said its blockbuster auction will go ahead as planned on Wednesday, despite a last-minute challenge by descendants of the artwork’s former owner.
articles.body: The sale of a Vincent van Gogh painting estimated to fetch $180 million at auction will proceed despite newly emerged claims that it was sold by a Jewish family “under duress” amid Nazi persecution in the 1930s. In a statement, Sotheby’s auction house said it is “aware of the concerns” raised about “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) by descendants of the artwork’s former owner but confirmed that the blockbuster sale will go ahead as planned on Wednesday evening. Unnamed heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher living in Berlin before World War II, have objected to the upcoming New York sale, arguing that their ancestors only sold the painting because of financial difficulties directly caused by the Nazi regime. Last Thursday, less than a week before the planned auction, their lawyer Gunnar Schnabel wrote to Sotheby’s urging it to prove beyond doubt that the painting was sold at market value — and that the family would have done so “even without Nazi rule,” according to correspondence seen by the New York Times. Schnabel, a Berlin-based lawyer specializing in Nazi-looted art, did not respond to CNN’s repeated requests for comment. “Sotheby’s takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of ‘Châtaigniers en fleurs,’” read Sotheby’s statement, sent to CNN on Monday, adding that the auction house has been “in dialogue” with Fischer’s heirs. “While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution,” the statement continued. This dispute is the latest in a string of art market controversies surrounding paintings that, although not confiscated by Nazis, may have been sold under pressure or below market rate during the Third Reich era. Schnabel — who has not disclosed the US-based heirs’ identities — told Sotheby’s that his clients are seeking a settlement “in the spirit of” the 1998 Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art, a series of international guidelines on resolving disputes over holocaust-era assets, according to the New York Times. Van Gogh painted “Châtaigniers en fleurs” in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise in 1890, shortly after his release from a psychiatric facility. In its catalog, Sotheby’s said the vibrant street scene demonstrated “magnificent brushwork and an exuberant, expressive range of colors.” Hungarian-born Fischer, founder of the publishing house S. Fischer Verlag, acquired it in Berlin in 1909. According to the Sotheby’s catalog, he deposited the painting with Paul Cassirer & Co., a gallery in Amsterdam, in either 1932 or 1933, the year the Nazi party came to power in Germany. Fischer died the next year, leaving his daughter and son-in-law, Brigitte and Gottfried Bermann-Fischer, in control of the family’s publishing house and his art collection. In June 1936, Paul Cassirer & Co. sold the painting — which was still, at the time, in the Netherlands — to the French collectors Marcel and Henriette Kapferer on the Bermann-Fischers’ behalf. By this time, the pair had already fled Berlin for Vienna, where they established an Austrian branch of the family’s publishing house. Schnabel reportedly believes this sale was necessitated by financial difficulties that the family business faced due to Nazi persecution. Some of the publisher’s high-profile authors, including Hermann Hesse and the Nobel Prize-winner Thomas Mann, had been blacklisted by the Nazi regime and their works ceremonially destroyed in book burnings. While the Bermann-Fischers successfully smuggled some of the family’s art collection to Austria (before resettling in Sweden and eventually the US), Schnabel found that they were forced to pay the “Reich flight tax,” a substantial levy placed on the assets of people fleeing Nazi Germany, the Times reported. Sotheby’s, meanwhile, believes there is no evidence that the sale was made under duress. The 1936 transaction was reportedly completed for 68,000 Swiss francs, then about $22,000. By comparison, Van Gogh’s painting “Verger avec cyprès,” which made history when it was sold for $117 million in 2022, sold for a reported $15,000 in 1935. “Châtaigniers en fleurs” remains poised to break the auction record for Van Gogh’s work, set by “Verger avec cyprès.” The painting had been guaranteed by Sotheby’s, meaning that the seller has been promised a minimum price for the item, regardless of what happens at the sale. The auction house has not disclosed this floor price, though a spokesperson told CNN that if the painting “sells on the night, it will likely make a record for the artist.” “Châtaigniers en fleurs” is one of 12 paintings — alongside works by Monet, Renoir and Cézanne — that Sotheby’s is offering from the collection of late Argentinian businessman Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his art patron wife, Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. It was purchased by the Blaquier-Arrieta family in 1975, having changed hands several times since World War II. In a statement issued via Sotheby’s, the Blaquier-Arrietas said they also welcome “constructive dialogue” with the Fischer heirs. “The family recognizes the importance of addressing concerns arising from the difficult circumstances of the Nazi era and respects the historical sensitivities involved,” the statement added. Because “Châtaigniers en fleurs” was sold in the Netherlands, which was not under Nazi occupation at the time, Fischer’s immediate heirs had little legal basis to seek compensation following World War II. But more recent — albeit non-binding — political agreements, including the 1998 Washington Principles and the 2009 Terezin Declaration (which explicitly references “forced sales and sales under duress”), have provided a new legal framework for descendants seeking restitution. In 2022, France’s government returned a Gustav Klimt painting to the heirs of a Jewish family forced to sell it at a reduced price after the Nazis annexed Austria in 1938. The following year, heirs of Jewish collectors Karl Adler and Rosi Jacobi filed a lawsuit against New York’s Guggenheim Museum over a Pablo Picasso painting that they claimed had been sold in desperation while their ancestors fled persecution, though the case was dismissed in 2024. Auction houses have typically avoided offering items that might fall foul of restitution claims, which can scare off potential buyers and attract criticism from Jewish advocacy groups. In 2023, amid growing public pressure, Sotheby’s rival Christie’s canceled a sale of around 300 pieces of jewelry from the collection of late art collector Heidi Horten, whose husband was accused of making his fortune by buying out Jewish businesses sold under duress in Nazi Germany.

articles.title: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts
articles.summary: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.
articles.body:
The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.

Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.

The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.

All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage . In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order .

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.

The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".

On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."

Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".

The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.

Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.

When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.

They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she told me in 2017 . Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.

Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.

Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.

Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.

Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.

In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".

"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.

"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."

Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".

"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.

In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

articles.title: As Knesset readies for new speaker, Israeli opposition holds powerful role
articles.summary: The anti-Netanyahu bloc holds the keys to electing a new parliamentary speaker, setting the momentum for change.
articles.body:
As soon as last month’s Israeli election results were clear, the political camp opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced it would work together to elect a new Knesset speaker right away.

In Israel’s current political climate, electing the Knesset speaker is not merely a procedural matter. Many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc hope it will usher in important changes to state institutions and create a positive momentum that would reflect on efforts by Gadi Eisenkot, now the de facto leader of the opposition, to form a government without Netanyahu, his coalition partners, or their legacy. These may be over-optimistic expectations.

A powerful position in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, could be a strategic asset for the Netanyahu opposition.

Under the law, the Knesset speaker has the power to set the agenda of the legislature, preside over proceedings, and manage the parliamentary process under the Knesset Rules of Procedure – including convening parliament for and presiding over a vote of confidence in the government.

Eisenkot and his political allies in the so-called “Change bloc” agreed on their nominees for speaker and the chairs of key committees. The request to hold a vote to elect the speaker was filed when the 26th Knesset was sworn in on November 10. The vote will be held in the Knesset on Tuesday.

Arab-led Israeli parties have pledged support to ensure a majority to elect Matan Kahana of Eisenkot’s Yashar party as speaker. The recently elected deputy speaker , Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Joint List, told Al Jazeera his powerful political alliance of Arab-majority parties would do whatever they need to support a change in the speaker of the Knesset. “We need to get rid of the Netanyahu coalition as soon as possible,” he added.

Matan Kahana recently joined Yashar, but he is not new to politics. He has served as an elected parliamentarian before, starting in 2019 as a member of former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s right-wing alliance, Yamina. In 2022, he was part of the National Unity alliance, a parliamentary bloc formed by Eisenkot and former Defense Minister Benny Gantz, among others.

Within the predominantly right-wing Netanyahu opposition bloc, Kahana is seen as someone who can forge working relationships and push ahead with the legislative agenda Change bloc voters supported.

Once a speaker is elected, the anti-Netanyahu bloc can make good on their promises. This includes introducing legislation to form an independent commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which the Netanyahu coalition has so far blocked despite the majority of Israelis backing it.

The anti-Netanyahu parties also want to restore the powers of the attorney general and reverse the Netanyahu coalition’s major changes that weaken the powers of the judiciary and, the opposition says, prevent effective oversight of the government.

Another piece legislation of concern to Netanyahu is a law that would impose a two-term limit on the premiership. This would disqualify Netanyahu from becoming prime minister again.

These important laws can be introduced and voted on while coalition negotiations continue and while Netanyahu is the caretaker prime minister.

However, Israelis who headed to the polls in historic numbers to end Netanyahu’s nearly two-decade grip on power will surely welcome the undoing of part of his legacy.

articles.title: 'I have never stolen': Mongolia's president announces resignation over $25 million bribery allegations
articles.summary: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa on Tuesday announced that he would step down following allegations that he received a $25 million bribe linked to a
articles.body: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa on Tuesday announced that he would step down following allegations that he received a $25 million bribe linked to a government railway contract awarded in 2019, when he was prime minister. Khurelsukh has denied wrongdoing but said he would cooperate with investigators and relinquish office so the allegations against him could be examined.“I have never stolen from my people or my state,” he said in a televised address to the nation. “I will hand over my duties as president and become an ordinary citizen.”The allegations were made by Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of the capital Ulaanbaatar and a member of the ruling Mongolian People's Party (MPP), but from a different faction within the party. He accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million in connection with the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project.The opposition Democratic Party subsequently demanded the president's resignation, saying the allegations reflected corruption and cronyism among leaders of the ruling party.Railway contract at centre of bribery allegationsThe accusations concern the awarding of a railway contract in 2019 to Bodi International LLC, one of Mongolia's largest conglomerates. Khurelsukh, who was prime minister at the time, is alleged to have ensured that the contract went to the company without a competitive bidding process and received money in return.Bodi International denied the allegations on Monday, saying it had not paid cash bribes to senior government officials or civil servants. The company described the accusations as defamatory and maintained that it had done nothing wrong.Two other senior officials named in the allegations also announced their resignations on Tuesday. They were Deputy Minister of Justice and Home Affairs Munkh-Erdene Dembereltseren and Cabinet Secretariat head Enkhbayar Battumur.Khurelsukh said he had faced sustained attacks on his reputation for more than a month. In his address, he said he agreed with the Democratic Party's demand that he step aside so the allegations could be investigated.“I will be investigated and will have my honour restored,” he said, according to the state-run Montsame news agency.Parliament must approve resignationKhurelsukh's announcement does not immediately remove him from office. Under Mongolian law, a presidential resignation must be approved by the 126-member State Great Khural, the country's unicameral parliament.The legislature is expected to meet later this week to consider his resignation. If it accepts the decision, the parliamentary speaker will serve as interim president.The resignation announcement comes amid divisions within the ruling MPP, which has been hit by internal power struggles in recent years. Mongolia has seen three prime ministers take office in just nine months, highlighting the instability within the governing party.Khurelsukh had also resigned as prime minister in January 2021 to contest the presidential election. He won the presidency six months later, while the MPP secured a majority in parliament.The current allegations have therefore opened a fresh political test for the ruling party and its leadership, with the president's future now dependent on parliament's decision and the outcome of the investigation.You use AI every day. articles.title: What Trump, Putin and Xi want from superpower summit
articles.summary: President Trump’s Asia trip will be capped by an unprecedented meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping — a nuclear-armed trilateral that harkens back to a more Machiavellian era of geopolitics. The summit, expected to take place Wednesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, is…
articles.body:
President Trump’s Asia trip will be capped by an unprecedented meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping — a nuclear-armed trilateral that harkens back to a more Machiavellian era of geopolitics.

The summit, expected to take place Wednesday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, is drawing rough comparisons to the Yalta Conference, when President Roosevelt met with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin to divide spheres of influence after World War II.

The agenda for this week’s meeting is murkier, but Trump says global conflict will again be at the center of talks, with the three powers discussing the fate of countries while excluding them from the discussion.

Trump is on the opposite side of Xi and Putin in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, though he has played down their support for Tehran. The U.S. under Trump has shifted toward Russia’s position in negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, but Washington continues to support Kyiv with intelligence, satellite access and U.S. arms purchased by Europe.

“On its face, declaring Shenzhen ‘Yalta 2’ is an awkward analogy,” Catherine Grace Katz, a historian and author of “The Daughters of Yalta: The Churchills, Roosevelts, and Harrimans: A Story of Love and War,” wrote in an article for LawFare.

“And yet, at a deeper, far more concerning level, Yalta may accidentally turn out to be exactly the right analogy for a summit among Trump, Putin, and Xi in November, particularly amid lapses in intelligence sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine and Trump’s decision to lift some sanctions on Russia, clear signals that the White House’s well of support for Ukraine may soon be running dry.”

Trump has indicated he wants to talk about Ukraine, Iran and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. He’s made little progress in finding areas of agreement or convergence on any of the issues, despite nearly two years of promising imminent breakthroughs.

The U.S. is the key backer of Ukraine’s more than four-year resistance to Russia’s intent to take over the country. And Russia would not be able to sustain its war against Ukraine if it wasn’t for China’s support.

Both Russia and China have provided Iran a variety of support — buying Iranian oil, selling dual-use military items and, reportedly, providing weapons — which has allowed Tehran to resist U.S. military and economic pressure. Russia has reportedly provided intelligence allowing Iran to hit U.S. bases.

And while Russia has earlier participated in nuclear nonproliferation talks with the U.S., China has shown little to no willingness to limit its nuclear weapons buildup. The Pentagon has assessed China will probably have more than 1,000 operational nuclear warheads by 2030.

A senior U.S. official said it was unlikely any deals or breakthroughs would come from the summit.

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” the official said Friday during a briefing with reporters. The meeting is the “entry point” and baseline for future, productive conversations, the official added.

Foreign policy experts agree there’s unlikely to be anything substantial.

“The meeting of these three leaders is the message,” Scott Kennedy, senior adviser in Chinese Business and Economics at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told the Singapore-based Channel NewsAsia .

“A message they all agree on, even if they don’t say it, is that great powers have a larger voice than smaller powers.”

For Putin, the image of him alongside Trump and Xi — who has called the Russian leader his “no limits” partner — demonstrates an elevated international position, even as Ukraine’s supporters in Europe and Asia have tried to alienate him. These countries argue any success Putin achieves in Ukraine will further embolden China to take over Taiwan.

“Holding such a meeting would give Putin another opportunity to argue that Western efforts to isolate Russia over its war in Ukraine have failed the test of time,” said Oleg Ignatov, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Russia.

Xi’s motivations are more complicated. He’s not likely to be interested in nuclear nonproliferation talks and is not involved in the U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.

“Beijing will approach the three-way summit with caution,” said William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia with the International Crisis Group.

While Xi can use the summit to demonstrate China as wielding strong convening power, the Chinese leader is likely to focus on “broad-scoped topics like global stability,” Yang noted.

“This approach would reflect Beijing’s efforts to minimize potential damage to its global image and relationship with European countries,” he said.

There are few signals that Putin or Xi are taking Trump’s talk of denuclearization seriously — or that any major preparatory work has taken place for a breakthrough or deal. But that shouldn’t exclude finding some way to progress nuclear weapons reduction, said Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association.

“Resuming progress on arms control and disarmament negotiations, bilaterally or multilaterally, is essential and this meeting is an important opportunity to begin to take the steps necessary to reduce the nuclear danger,” Kimball said in an email to The Hill.

Kimball said there are concrete steps the three leaders can take. The first is to agree to launch talks for a new agreement to cap and freeze nuclear arsenals.

Trump, Xi and Putin could also reaffirm a ban on nuclear weapons testing, part of commitments under the 1996 Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. All three countries have signed the document but not ratified it. They could also launch technical talks to guard against “clandestine, low-yield nuclear explosions,” before the treaty enters into force.

Third, the leaders could reinforce commitments to maintain human control over decisions about nuclear weapons in the face of risks posed by artificial intelligence.

A senior U.S. official said China should “step up to the adult’s table” and engage in hard talks about its nuclear weapons arsenal.

“The world is very much a place that we share, and that the things that China is doing very opaquely with their nuclear arsenals are something that have impacts on the security of every human being in the world,” the official added.

The trilateral summit will conclude Trump’s trip in Asia, heightening the pressure on America’s democratic partners in the region to exert influence on the president in meetings beforehand.

Trump is set to attend a leader-level meeting with the heads of the other three countries that make up the Quad — Japan, India and Australia — on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila. It will be the first Quad gathering in two years.

The Quad is viewed as a preeminent security grouping contesting China’s ambition in the region. But Trump’s lack of focus on the group, and tensions with India over trade deals, have weakened the Quad, experts say.

The meeting will be particularly important for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, whose country is on the front line of provocation from both China and Russia, which are increasing joint naval drills and military exercises surrounding Japan.

Japan is the “linchpin” of U.S. security in Asia, said a former U.S. official, requesting anonymity because of the sensitivity of the topic.

“I don’t think it is just the issue of what issues are described or discussed in the meeting. It is the meeting itself and then the surrounding choreography,” the former official said.

“The most important thing that President Trump can do in China is have a warm, good meeting with Prime Minister Takaichi.”

articles.title: Bangladesh police clash with garment workers amid protests over wages
articles.summary: Protesters hurl bricks, torch vehicles and block the main highway between Dhaka and Mymensingh.
articles.body:
Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.

Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district of Mymensingh.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for big international brands, including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.

But growing worker unrest over wages, which began last month, has disrupted the industry that generates $38bn annually and employs more than four million people.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) – a 140-percent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.

About 500 of the country’s 4,500 garment factories are shut, sources told the AFP news agency, further stoking unrest among workers.

A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” one worker, Khanom, 24, told AFP.

Tensions were also running high in the garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on Dhaka’s outskirts.

The wage board , comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.

The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January next year.

“We want to return to our machines,” garment worker Rakib, 28, told AFP.

“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.

Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning, but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.

In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.

A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a BGMEA source told AFP.

The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.

In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.

“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.

The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

articles.title: From Russia-Ukraine war to Iran-US conflict: The return of the 'dirty bomb' threat
articles.summary: US intelligence agencies have detected what officials describe as Iranian planning to potentially target senior members of President Donald Trump's
articles.body: US intelligence agencies have detected what officials describe as Iranian planning to potentially target senior members of President Donald Trump's administration in Washington DC using a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon, according to a CNN report citing seven US officials.The intelligence has triggered contingency planning in the United States, although officials remain divided over whether Iran has the capability or intention to carry out such an attack. Sources familiar with the assessment said the planning appeared to be an effort by Tehran to keep its options open rather than evidence of an imminent operationTwo sources cited by CNN claimed that the alleged plotting included specific locations and potential targets. US officials have also held several meetings over the past week to discuss ways to counter the threat.However, Iran's foreign ministry denied the report and termed the allegations as 'baseless'.White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the administration was monitoring potential threats but added that “at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland”.The Iranian Mission to the United Nations in New York rejected allegations concerning chemical weapons, saying Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard”. The statement did not explicitly address the intelligence about a possible dirty bomb plan.The reported threat comes as the US and Iran remain locked in conflict, with Washington continuing military strikes and an economic blockade against Tehran. Diplomatic efforts to end the hostilities have made little progress.Against this backdrop, the alleged planning has renewed attention on dirty bombs, which are different from nuclear weapons but can spread radioactive material over populated areas.What is a dirty bomb and how does it work?A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersion device, combines conventional explosives with radioactive material. When the explosive detonates, it scatters the radioactive substance into the surrounding environment through dust, smoke and debris.Unlike a nuclear bomb, a dirty bomb does not trigger a nuclear-fission reaction. It does not produce a nuclear explosion capable of destroying an entire city. Instead, its purpose is to disperse radioactive contamination, potentially forcing people to evacuate affected areas and disrupting normal life.The device is considered relatively crude and easier to assemble than a nuclear weapon. It does not necessarily require sophisticated technology, although obtaining radioactive material remains a key challenge.Radioactive substances used in medicine, industrial equipment and research facilities could potentially be used in such a device.The quantity and type of radioactive material, the strength of the conventional explosive and weather conditions, particularly wind direction, would determine how widely contamination spreads.In 2022, the term “dirty bomb” became a talking point during the Russia-Ukraine war after Moscow accused Kyiv of preparing to use such a device on its own territory.Ukraine rejected the allegation, calling it false, while the United States and its Western allies dismissed Russia’s claims as an attempt to create a pretext for escalation.The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) subsequently carried out inspections at three Ukrainian locations identified by Russia and found no indications of undeclared nuclear activities or materials.How dangerous can a dirty bomb be?The immediate casualties from a dirty bomb would largely depend on the conventional explosion rather than radiation exposure, experts say. While radioactive material can cause harm, most such devices would not release enough radiation to kill large numbers of people or cause severe illness across a wide area.However, radioactive dust and smoke can be dangerous, particularly when inhaled close to the blast site. The material could contaminate buildings, public infrastructure and surrounding areas, requiring evacuations and costly clean-up operations.The extent of contamination would depend on the radioactive substance used and how it disperses. In some scenarios, affected buildings and public spaces could remain inaccessible for extended periods.The economic consequences could be substantial even if the immediate health impact was limited. Evacuations, restrictions on access to urban areas and decontamination work could disrupt businesses and public services.The psychological impact is also a major concern. Since radiation cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, people may not know whether they have been exposed. Detecting contamination requires specialised equipment.For this reason, dirty bombs are often described as weapons of terror or mass disruption rather than precision weapons.Why are US officials concerned about the alleged Iranian plans?According to CNN, US intelligence has picked up Iranian communications claiming that bomb-making materials have been stored inside the United States. However, officials remain divided over how credible that information is.Sources familiar with the intelligence told CNN that Iran may not need to bring trained operatives into the country to carry out an attack. It could potentially persuade someone already living in the US to execute a plot.One official said the capability to carry out such an attack had not necessarily increased, but that Iran's incentive to consider one may have changed amid the conflict.US officials are also monitoring separate intelligence suggesting that Iran could use chemical weapons against American troops stationed in the Middle East. The concerns have prompted parallel contingency planning to ensure diplomatic and intelligence personnel in the region have appropriate protective equipment and training.The report also highlighted concerns about the availability of protective equipment and training for US troops in the region.What happens if a dirty bomb is detonated?The response to a suspected dirty bomb attack would involve identifying the radioactive material, assessing the extent of contamination and restricting access to affected areas.Specialised equipment would be needed to detect radiation and determine which locations require evacuation or decontamination. Emergency teams would also have to assess the risks to people who may have inhaled or come into contact with radioactive particles.The scale of the response would depend on the type and quantity of material released, the area affected and the level of exposure.As per news agency AP, radioactive contamination could make homes, businesses and public facilities unusable until they had undergone expensive clean-up operations.Depending on the material involved, restrictions could last for months or longer.The primary challenge, therefore, may not necessarily be the number of people killed by radiation but the disruption caused by contamination, evacuation and the difficulty of restoring affected areas to normal use.
