articles.title: Gleneagles Hotel buys Scotland's 'ghost' golf course
articles.summary: The gWest course in Blackford was completed in 2009, but never officially opened to the public.
articles.body:
The Gleneagles Hotel has bought a neighbouring "ghost" golf resort, which has been shrouded in secrecy for years, for an undisclosed sum.

The gWest course in Blackford, Perth and Kinross, was completed in 2009 but never officially opened to the public and very few people are thought to have played it.

The Gleneagles Hotel said the purchase offered an opportunity to "extend our stewardship of this remarkable landscape that has always been integral to the spirit of the hotel."

The course was previously owned by Mahdi al-Tajir, the owner of mineral water firm Highland Spring who was previously Scotland's richest man, and his family.

He made his money in oil but the golf course business was listed in three of his sons' names.

The 639-acre estate includes an 18-hole championship course and a clubhouse shell, as well as planning consent for up to 170 residential plots, a hotel and spa, leisure and entertainment facilities, and staff accommodation.

The resort's website describes it as "Scotland's best-kept secret".

A Gleneagles Hotel spokesperson said: "Surrounded by the rolling Ochil Hills and breathtaking scenery, this land shares the same natural beauty and character that has defined the Gleneagles Hotel for over a century.

"Nestled within this landscape is a golf course quietly whispered about, one of the lesser-known treasures of Perthshire."

The spokesperson said the hotel looked forward to sharing more information "as our plans take shape, guided by the same care and consideration that have shaped this special place for over a century".

The golf course was originally just one aspect of plans for the site which included luxury homes and a seven-star hotel, according to local people who spoke BBC Radio 4 podcast The Patch .

But the global financial crisis, Scotland's independence referendum and Brexit were cited for the lack of progress.

articles.title: A Melbourne woman spent A$2,000 on four Apple gift cards at Coles, but discovered their redemption codes were scratched out; the supermarket initially refused a refund before agreeing to return her money
articles.summary: A Melbourne woman who spent A$2,000 on four Apple gift cards at Coles discovered that their redemption codes had been scratched out, leaving her unable to
articles.body: A Melbourne woman who spent A$2,000 on four Apple gift cards at Coles discovered that their redemption codes had been scratched out, leaving her unable to use the vouchers. The purchase, which initially appeared to be a way to earn extra Flybuys points, turned into a frustrating dispute after supermarket staff reportedly refused to refund the money. The retailer eventually reversed its decision and agreed to return the amount. The incident later became part of a wider ABC News investigation into tampered gift cards being sold across Australia.Melbourne woman's A$2,000 Apple gift cards found with scratched-out codesAccording to an ABC News investigation report published on May 21, 2026, Melbourne-based illustrator Georgia Perry bought four Apple gift cards from a Coles supermarket in Yarraville, an inner-western suburb of Melbourne. Each card was worth A$500, bringing the total purchase to A$2,000.Perry had purchased the vouchers on a Tuesday evening because she wanted to buy a new iPhone. An in-store promotion offering 20 times the usual Flybuys points on Apple gift card purchases also made the deal appear attractive.However, the purchase took an unexpected turn when she returned home and began opening the cards. The first voucher appeared to have no usable redemption code, with the area where the code should have been showing signs of scratching or peeling. Initially, Perry thought she might have damaged it while removing the card from its packaging.The same problem appeared on the remaining three cards. All four vouchers had their redemption codes scratched out, making them unusable for the intended purchase.Why did Coles initially refuse to refund the moneyPerry took the four vouchers back to the supermarket after discovering the damage. However, she told ABC News that the store staff were unwilling to help and reportedly explained that they could not take responsibility because gift cards were third-party products.She also contacted Apple for assistance. During the process, the company's helpline asked her to provide photographs of the cards, including their serial numbers. This revealed another problem, as the final digits on the cards had also been scratched out.Perry subsequently lodged a formal complaint with Coles. The supermarket confirmed receiving it and said its customer care team had responded within an hour and continued working towards a resolution.The initial response left Perry dissatisfied. She described the customer service experience as uninterested and lacking urgency. She also questioned how the cards could have reached the shop floor in that condition, particularly because the damage was not obvious while they remained attached to their cardboard packaging.How did Coles eventually agree to return the A$2,000The situation changed after Perry shared a video of her experience on Instagram. Her complaint attracted widespread attention, receiving more than 150,000 views by the morning after it was posted, alongside hundreds of comments from people discussing gift card fraud and consumer rights.According to ABC News, a Coles employee left Perry a voicemail confirming that a refund would be issued. Emails reviewed by the ABC team showed that the gift card supplier had deactivated the A$2,000 worth of vouchers and returned the money to Coles.The supermarket subsequently informed Perry that she was eligible for a refund and apologised for the poor experience.What did the ABC investigation discover about gift card fraudIn an extensive investigation published on August 31, 2026, ABC News revealed that shoppers across Australia had reported buying gift cards with missing or damaged redemption codes from major supermarket chains.The investigation examined 19 reports of suspicious gift cards, many involving Apple vouchers. It reviewed customer receipts, photographs of damaged cards and correspondence with retailers, Apple and gift card distributors.The earliest reports identified by the ABC dated back to 2024. That year, a Coles customer in Perth and a Woolworths shopper in Sydney reported problems with their purchases.The ABC investigation identified another customer, Lavkesh Arora, who bought five Apple gift cards worth A$2,000 from a Coles store in the city’s eastern suburbs. Two of the cards worth A$700 combined, had missing redemption codes and digits. Another shopper, Damian Toohey, reported finding a scratched-off number on an Apple gift card purchased from Woolworths.How does the gift card tampering scam operateThe ABC investigation also examined how criminals could tamper with physical gift cards before returning them to supermarket shelves.Adam Parks, a former Australian representative of the US Department of Homeland Security's investigative unit, explained that the practice is commonly known in the industry as card draining.According to Parks, the process can involve people taking gift cards from shop shelves, carefully opening their packaging and recording the information needed to access the funds. They may use razor blades or hair dryers to remove the packaging without leaving obvious signs of damage.The cards are then returned to their packaging and placed back on supermarket shelves. When an unsuspecting customer purchases one, the retailer activates it at the checkout.The stolen information can then be used to monitor the card's balance and activation status. Once a customer pays for the voucher, those involved in the scam may spend its value before the buyer gets an opportunity to redeem it.This can make the fraud difficult to identify immediately. Gift cards are frequently purchased as presents, meaning some customers might not open them for weeks or months after the original transaction.Parks told ABC News that the operation becomes profitable when carried out on a large scale, with different people potentially handling the collection, tampering and use of the stolen information.Are Australian supermarkets taking steps to prevent the problemThe ABC investigation found that Coles had previously worked with police to address gift card tampering. Court documents revealed that a man was arrested after allegedly placing tampered Apple gift cards on shelves on at least 5 Coles stores in Sydney.Police alleged that the cards involved were worth at least A$10,200. The man was sentenced to a two-year community corrections order and a 15-month suspended sentence.Both Coles and Woolworths acknowledged the wider problem and defended their efforts to prevent it. Woolworths was trialling anti-tamper hangers and staffed stations near gift card displays in some stores.Apple had also changed its Australian gift card packaging in early 2025. The newer design included perforated edges intended to make signs of opening or interference easier to identify. Its packaging also carried a warning against buying or selling cards that appeared to have been tampered with.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on U.S. targets in Bahrain
articles.summary: Iran fired drones across the Persian Gulf on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom as Tehran resumed strikes on its Arab neighbors after a roughly two-month lull.
articles.body: Iran fired drones across the Persian Gulf on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom as Tehran resumed strikes on its Arab neighbors after a roughly two-month lull. After issuing an alert of the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the “treacherous Iranian aerial attacks.” The attack came after the U.S. military’s Central Command confirmed that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group had arrived in the region. The move adds a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the American presence as U.S. President Donald Trump keeps his options open for his next move in the war, which began nearly nine months ago. The combined U.S. naval assets in the Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel conducted joint strikes on Iran to launch the war on Feb. 28 — the presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies. The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn’t comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region or replace the Washington, which had been redeployed from the Asia-Pacific region to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concerns of its lengthy deployment. The Washington itself has now been deployed for around six months. Iran’s attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done. The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said that they were done in retaliation. “Continued aggression against the country’s airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran will not go unanswered,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement. The U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the recent attacks. With negotiations stagnating on bringing an end to the war, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar, the latest military developments have further complicated prospects for a negotiated settlement, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, in an analysis posted to X. As the U.S. mulls whether to resume all-out military attacks on Iran or to intensify its blockade to further sap strength from Iran’s economy, Iranian leaders will also now be weighing whether “breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation,” Azizi wrote. “In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again,” he said. “It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation.” The attacks on the American facilities in Bahrain are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient with the waiting game as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation,” Bruchmann told The Associated Press. “Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn’t overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet.” Iranian officials have termed the current situation “no war, no peace” and vowed that it must be brought to an end. Tehran has said that it’s open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran’s economy. Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic “security crisis.” He said that the strikes on Bahrain were meant “to prevent the gradual expansion of enemy operations and to impose costs on its military infrastructure.” Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. Before the war, ships had freely passed through the key waterway, carrying about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas. Since then, Iran has held a tight grip on the strait and only a fraction of the peacetime shipping traffic has been able to pass through, despite U.S. efforts to provide escorts. On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board. Iran’s Fars news agency also reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn’t immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military’s UKMTO. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated on the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition. Those government-allied forces are now fortifying their defenses in areas leading to the southern city of Aden, which serves as an interim capital of the internationally recognized government, two Yemeni military officials said. Their efforts are focused on deploying more troops and equipment in and around the district of Tur al-Baha in the southern province of Lahij, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media.

articles.title: Will the College Football Playoff selection committee embarrass itself again with new rankings? | Ian Miller
articles.summary: Curt Cignetti ripped the College Football Playoff committee as Indiana fell five spots on a bye, while every Alabama Crimson Tide SEC win lost Saturday.
articles.body: We've had two weeks of the College Football Playoff selection committee's top-25 poll, and two weeks of well-deserved controversy over their rankings. And the controversy extends well past just the positions each team sits, to the reasoning behind it. Both weeks have had one consistent theme: the SEC has received an enormous, and undeserved, boost for their teams. Losses don't count for as much in the SEC, while every win is assumed to be a "quality" one. Injuries are given more deference, and preseason expectations are still treated as meaningful. All while teams in other conferences are punished for ... not playing. Like the Indiana Hoosiers, who dropped five spots in the rankings from No. 4 to No. 9 while on a bye week. HERE'S HOW BAD THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF'S SELECTION COMMITTEE RANKINGS ACTUALLY ARE Head coach Curt Cignetti, the defending national champion, brought up how many other coaches are thinking and feeling about the poll in a Monday press conference. Roasting the selection committee for the disparate treatment and how they handle losses and wins dependent on brand names, stadiums, and marketing efforts, not team quality. "You get tired of the narrative sometimes," Cignetti said. "A quality win because Joe Smith was playing at the time. They ain’t won a game since, but it was a quality win back then. I guess bad losses don’t count. Look, it’s all going to play out on the field. It’s good for entertainment. I’m sure this’ll get a lot of nice hits and play. "But our guys understand that it’ll play out on the field. The good thing about it is, I think it feeds into our motivation and our chip. That’s why I’m not afraid to keep it alive. And you know what? I’m 65 years old and I really don’t give a s--t." How the committee handled Cignetti's Indiana team is one thing. How they justify it is another. And that justification is why the committee faces a major test of their legitimacy and remaining shreds of credibility. NEW COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF POLL PROVES THE SELECTION COMMITTEE IS JUST MAKING IT UP AS THEY GO During committee chair Hunter Yurachek's post-release interview, he "explained" why the Hoosiers fell five spots without playing. "Indiana was probably a victim of having a bye week at the wrong time with seven games between Top 25 teams," he said. "The committee is really impressed with what UCLA, Texas, and Notre Dame did as well as Alabama and LSU." "Every team that Indiana had played to date in the Big Ten all lost and that affected their strength of schedule rank and the committee's review of Indiana," he continued. "The quarterback play in general and the offensive play in general is kind of a discussion point of Indiana ... They've won games because of their defense and not their offense." As ridiculous as it is to knock a team for having an elite defense, that wasn't the worst of it. DAKICH: LANE KIFFIN HAS TURNED LSU INTO A LAUGHING STOCK - LISTEN NOW This is: "every team that Indiana had played to date in the Big Ten all lost and that affected their strength of schedule rank." First, we have no idea how the committee evaluates the strength of schedule, because there is no transparency around what metrics they use, or even if they just make it up as they go and don't use any. But the problem is that Yurachek made it clear that Indiana's opponents all losing, hurt their strength of schedule in the eyes of the committee. Well, we've got good news for them, because they have an opportunity to demonstrate their consistency and lack of favoritism this week. With their beloved Alabama Crimson Tide. Let's take a quick look at how Alabama's prior SEC wins did this week: CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Well then! Isn't that interesting. All five of Alabama's non-Vanderbilt wins lost on Saturday, four of them at home in the Awe-Inspiring Cathedral, which is an SEC stadium. Those five teams are now a combined 27-23, and eight of those wins came against Kent State, Towson, Louisiana-Monroe, Youngstown State, Louisiana Tech, McNeese State, Missouri State and The Citadel. So will the committee stay true to their word and penalize the Tide for all of their "quality SEC wins" losing over the weekend? Then there's an argument to be made that Alabama deserves to move down because their win over Vanderbilt might have been less impressive than Indiana sitting at home. They had just 4.5 yards per play on offense against one of the worst defenses in the conference and the 110th worst defense in FBS when it comes to points allowed. Take out three plays of 20+ yards and they gained 227 on 65 plays, an average of just 3.49 per play. Their touchdown drive in the third quarter was 12 yards, after a long kickoff return. And they were fortunate to go into halftime leading after a flag on 3rd-and-9 set up a touchdown instead of a field goal. It was about as unimpressive as a win can be. And all their SEC wins lost on the same weekend. So will the committee move them down five or six spots? Somehow it seems doubtful, doesn't it? This is, after all, the same organization that put the Tide in the 12-team tournament last year after getting obliterated in the SEC Championship Game. Alabama's only two games against top-10 opponents, Georgia and Tennessee, they lost. In 2025, we were told that Notre Dame didn't deserve to make the tournament because they lost two games against top quality opponents, Miami and Texas A&M. Interesting! The entire SEC took a major hit this weekend, with many of its supposedly good teams losing. Ole Miss is now 6-4 after a bad loss to a mediocre Oklahoma team. Texas A&M is 1-6 in the SEC and 4-6 overall. Missouri, which seems to exist solely to be ranked in the 20s in order to provide a "ranked win" for other teams, got annihilated by Georgia and fell to 6-4. They'll probably still be ranked, but nobody outside the selection committee room thinks they deserve it. LSU is now 6-4 and 3-4 in the SEC. South Carolina, which inexplicably moved up to No. 17 last week, was blown out by a very bad Arkansas team to drop to 6-4. Mississippi State, which still gets treated as a patented "quality win" because of the injury to Kamario Taylor, showed that they are not, in fact, a quality team, losing 41-9 to Auburn. The Bulldogs defense, which does not include Kamario Taylor, has now given up 56 to Bama, lost 31-0 to LSU, 23 points to Oklahoma, 31 to Texas, 25 to Vanderbilt, and 41 to Auburn. Nearly 35 points per game as they've fallen to 4-6. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD None of this is to say that Alabama isn't a good team deserving of a playoff spot. Based on underlying performance and predictive metrics, they are clearly one of the best 5–10 teams in the country. But when the committee sets out its "standards" in plain English, it warrants monitoring how they live up to them if one of their favorite teams is affected. Will the committee stop overrating the SEC now? Will they stop giving them the benefit of the doubt? That's the question facing them on Tuesday night. And how they answer it will determine how much credibility they have left. It probably won't be much.

articles.title: Seattle Times still hasn't corrected claim that trans women have no athletic advantage despite studies
articles.summary: The Seattle Times says no serious evidence favors trans girls in sports, but Jason Rantz and Benjamin Ryan cite studies showing athletic advantages.
articles.body: The Seattle Times wasted little time. The morning after independent journalist Nick Shirley retracted his allegation that Lam's Seafood Asian Market — a staple of Seattle's International District — had engaged in EBT fraud, the newspaper published a story about it. It was exactly the kind of article the Times should have been writing, as Shirley's dubious claims threatened the livelihood of the family that owns the business, which maintained it had been wrongly accused. JACKSON THOMPSON: SEATTLE SCHOOL BOARD AUTHORIZES LEGAL CHALLENGE TO BALLOT MEASURE PROTECTING GIRLS' SPORTS Holding journalists accountable for their mistakes is precisely what newspapers are supposed to do. But what happens when it's The Seattle Times making the dubious claims? Seems the same standards don't apply. On Nov. 8, the Times published a story examining why Washington voters overwhelmingly supported Initiative 638, which would prohibit biological males from competing in girls' K-12 sports. And as I've said before, the paper deserves credit for including voices on both sides of the issue. But midway through the piece came a paragraph that made me wonder how many editors had actually read it. "There is no serious scientific evidence that trans girls or women are better athletes than cisgender girls or women. A few transgender girls have won at the high school level, but across the U.S., just a few trans women have competed at elite college or professional levels, and none have dominated their sport." Since then, a slew of writers have challenged the Times' assertion, pointing to scientific research that suggests otherwise. PABLO TORRE SAYS NCAA HAS NO TRANSGENDER ATHLETES, CONVENIENTLY LEAVES OUT THE REASON WHY Seattle Red radio host Jason Rantz cited a 2020 study of U.S. Air Force personnel showing that transgender women were still 12% faster than biological females in a 1.5-mile run after two years of hormone therapy. Investigative journalist Benjamin Ryan, meanwhile, reposted an old Substack essay that linked to a 2025 scientific paper finding that substantial advantages in strength, power, size and aerobic capacity can remain after testosterone suppression. He also cited a 2020 review showing that transgender women typically lose just 5% of their muscle mass after a year of hormone therapy. RACHEL MADDOW SAYS TRANS SPORTS DEBATE IS A MADE UP ISSUE TO HARM TRANS PEOPLE Then there was former New York Times and current Sport and State writer Karen Crouse, who cited a 2021 review finding that strength, lean mass and muscle size remained above female levels even after three years of hormone treatment. She also pointed to a 2023 American College of Sports Medicine consensus statement documenting the performance advantages males typically develop during puberty. That's a lot of scientific evidence for something the Times says doesn't exist. And yet...no retraction, clarification or editor's note. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! It's not like the paper's brass is unaware of the criticism, which has been all over social media. Ryan showed me a screenshot of one of the story's reporters thanking him for his feedback before saying, "I've shared this with our team." Krouse wrote that she reached out to multiple editors for clarification but received no response. Monday, I emailed the Times' executive editor, managing editor and PR representative for comment but did not hear back. Included in my email were links to the aforementioned writers' critiques followed by this question: "Could it be that the Times doesn't consider this evidence to be 'serious'?" What would worry me, if I were the publisher, is whether fewer and fewer people are viewing that paper as serious. To publish a claim contradicted by peer-reviewed research and then leave repeated requests for clarification unanswered is a study in either pride or cowardice. Perhaps both. Journalists make mistakes. I've made plenty myself. But those mistakes should be followed by accountability, not avoidance. articles.title: Cornell to examine future of Greek life after report of gang rape at a fraternity house
articles.summary: Cornell University will launch a sweeping review of its Greek system and its future on campus after a report of a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024, the university’s president said.
articles.body: Cornell University will launch a sweeping review of its Greek system and its future on campus after a report of a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024, the university’s president said Monday. The review will focus on the Greek system’s relationship to housing and residential life, President Michael Kotlikoff said in a letter to the Cornell community. Details will be announced in the coming weeks, he said. The announcement marks the university’s latest response to outrage over its handling of a woman’s report that she was drugged and sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The woman, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men in September. Cornell expelled or suspended several students after an internal investigation and barred the fraternity chapter from campus. The accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged. Kotlikoff has faced criticism for his handling of the case, including his acknowledgment that he never read the campus police report and did not follow up on the outcome of the investigations. He has defended the university’s disciplinary process and said administrators were prohibited from interfering in criminal investigations. Cornell previously suspended parties at fraternities and announced additional measures to prevent sexual violence on campus. “To prevent sexual assault, we must reshape the social environments, interactions, and physical spaces that can contribute to increased risk,” Kotlikoff wrote Monday. He also outlined plans to expand sexual assault prevention education, create more late-night social opportunities outside residential spaces and establish an academic center dedicated to researching campus sexual violence. The university said it is exploring ways to revitalize businesses and develop public gathering places in Collegetown, a neighborhood near campus where many students live and socialize. Jane Doe’s lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and Whitney Seals, said in a statement that while they welcomed action by Cornell’s administrators to address sexual assault on campus, “words, task forces, and prospective reviews cannot erase years of institutional inaction.” “Jane Doe welcomes any genuine effort that prevents another student from enduring what she suffered. However, meaningful reform requires full transparency into how past reports of sexual violence were mishandled, real consequences for those responsible, and a permanent end to a culture that prioritizes institutional reputation over student safety,” they said. The announcement comes just over a week after Cornell’s Faculty Senate passed a vote of no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address sexual assault on campus. In his letter Monday, Kotlikoff directly acknowledged the loss of confidence in Cornell’s administration. “I know many in our community have lost confidence in the Cornell administration’s ability to prevent and respond to sexual violence,” he wrote. “You have raised necessary questions about what the administration is doing to keep our students safe and where we have fallen short.” Kotlikoff pledged more regular communication about the university’s efforts, including a new public accountability dashboard tracking its progress. Meanwhile, an independent review led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates is underway. Kotlikoff said its findings would guide longer-term changes to how Cornell investigates and adjudicates allegations of sexual misconduct.

articles.title: Bahrain intercepts Iranian drones targeting US radar after 2-month lull in Gulf strikes
articles.summary: Iran's IRGC claims it struck a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, home to the Fifth Fleet, the third attack in five days after a lull.
articles.body: Iran fired drones toward what it said was a U.S. military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday, marking the third strike in five days after a roughly two-month lull in the conflict, Reuters reported. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its target was the radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, which is home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet. Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted the incoming drones after authorities issued a security alert urging residents to seek shelter. Officials announced an all-clear later in the morning, with no deaths or injuries reported. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also addressed the Iranian drone strikes, saying they didn't hit their intended target. The drones were "intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," CENTCOM said. IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS The attempted attack followed another wave of Iranian aerial strikes that Bahrain repelled on Sunday, when the IRGC claimed six of its drones targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. That strike came two days after Friday's initial attempt against a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain — the first major attack after the two-month pause. U.S. Central Command said American forces shot down both drones in that incident, with no casualties or injuries. Reuters previously reported that President Donald Trump has told advisors that he may not attack Iran again if there are no more provocations from the IRGC or the Houthis, an Iran-backed terrorist group in Yemen. TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING Trump has said he plans to maintain the naval blockade on Iran, essentially putting the country's economy into a vice grip. He said the blockade will remain in place as long as Tehran seeks to disrupt traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. In recent days, attacks on tankers have increased in the strait, still one of the world's most vital transit routes for global energy supplies. articles.title: Iranians fear more civilian infrastructure could be targeted in new US war
articles.summary: Energy facilities, industrial units, ports and bridges, schools, hospitals and apartment buildings have already been hit
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranians say they are concerned about United States media reports that civilian infrastructure could be hit if the US launches a new war on Iran.

The New York Times published an investigative report on Monday claiming some overlap between dam building in Iran and suspected underground missile sites , as well as military demand for water and electricity.

The report acknowledged that the connection remains speculative, but has received backlash for linking civilian infrastructure to the military.

Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, civilian infrastructure in Iran has been extensively damaged in air attacks, impacting energy supplies, logistics, and the economy.

Navid, a 34-year-old resident of Tehran who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that after his experiences in the war, “it’s worrying how easily conversations have shifted to talking about attacking fundamental things like water, electricity and gas.”

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the report was “preparing the next round” of attacks on civilian infrastructure.

“Cool. New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” read a post on his X account.

Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, CEO of the London-based Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, said fewer than 50 of Iran’s more than 500 large dams have turbines installed to generate electricity.

“The reason there are so many dams in Iran is because there are vested interests, including IRGC construction companies, that use infrastructure budgets to generate rents,” he explained on X.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, also highlighted “recent acts of aggression by the USrael [sic] against Iran, water storage reservoirs”.

“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” he wrote on X.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to destroy Iranian power plants and bridges in the event of a new war and said he was “not at all” concerned that such attacks could constitute war crimes. Last week, Trump said all key infrastructure in Iran could be “wiped out” in three days, beginning with bridges. Trump has also warned that US forces are “fully locked and loaded” and have 38 bridges in their crosshairs.

The US has already been strongly criticised by Tehran for bombing a girls’ school in Minab on the first day of the war, killing 120 children.

Airwars, a United Kingdom-based nonprofit that tracks civilian harm in conflict-affected nations, documented almost 1,000 “incidents of harm”, where at least one person was killed in acts of violence across the Middle East, during the first 40 days of the war.

US-based rights groups in April, during the height of the war, reported that 1,701 civilians had been killed in the US-Israel assault on Iran, ‌including at least 254 children.

Given their experiences during the war, Iranians have been concerned about the prospect of more civilian sites being targeted.

Mostafa Najafi, a political analyst close to the security establishment, also believes the “targeted and inhumane” media report seeks to normalise attacks on civilian targets, which could undermine social stability in Iran.

“By turning an unverified coincidence in timing and geographical overlap into a security hypothesis, this report has laid the groundwork for suggesting that some of Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including water-transfer projects, forms part of a military support network,” he wrote in a social media post.

“Undoubtedly, this narrative framework could influence future debates about the nature of military and civilian targets and the legitimacy of attacking Iran’s critical infrastructure.”

The Tasnim and Mehr news websites, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also similarly described the investigation as an engineered report intended to justify attacks.

A number of the experts quoted in the investigation said later they do not support attacks on civilian infrastructure, or the hypothesis that dams are directly supporting military projects.

“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” said Kaveh Madani, director of the UN University’s water institute, who is also a former deputy head of Iran’s Department of Environment.

“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles!” he wrote on X. “This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure”.

During both the 12-day war of June 2025 and the current war starting on February 28, civilian infrastructure – often claimed to be “dual use” – has been widely targeted in air attacks.

Oil, gas and petrochemical facilities in southern Iran, oil depots across Tehran, a power plant in Khorramshahr, as well as a desalination plant in Qeshm and water reservoirs in Fars and Khuzestan have been attacked.

The B1 bridge in Karaj near Tehran, among the biggest in the Middle East, was extensively damaged just days before opening to traffic. Multiple bridges were destroyed in Bandar Khamir in southern Hormozgan, while the Bandar Abbas railway junction in the south and Aq Tekeh Khan railway bridge to the north were struck to create disruptions.

Steel and aluminium factories, airports, commercial ports and fishing infrastructure, hospitals and emergency services, medicines manufacturing and public-health research centres, apartment buildings, schools and universities were also among the targets.

Iran’s armed forces have launched missile and drone attacks at civilians and military sites across the Arab world, including the Ras Laffan LNG production facilities in Qatar, and refineries, airports and other facilities.

Iran’s leadership has promised it will pursue “maximum deterrence” through an unfettered response without geographical limits if the country is attacked again.

Despite ongoing mediated negotiations, Iran and the US continue to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, where the IRGC struck multiple vessels attempting “unauthorised” routes over the past day.

The IRGC also said it attacked a US radar system at Sheikh Isa Airbase in Bahrain on Tuesday in what it called a response to lingering US violations of Iranian airspace.

articles.title: Alexander Skarsgård perfects the art of the going-out top
articles.summary: Skarsgård wore a shimmering Tom Ford “going-out top” at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles.
articles.body: It has been hard to miss Alexander Skarsgård lately. The “Wicker” actor has had a winning streak of playful red carpet and press looks that have all been lessons in how to cheekily honor his co-star, be a baby, or wear a freaky little shoe. On Sunday at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles, his fashion instruction continued with a course on how to style the perfect going-out top. Wearing a layered head-to-toe look from Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann, the ensemble included a shimmering low-cut shirt and crystal-embroidered waistcoat beneath a black wool double-breasted jacket with a black orchid motif. The going-out top was a millennial style staple throughout the 2000s. Any sequined, zippered or otherwise embellished tank or halter that could be paired with pants or a skirt and worn out for happy hour or a late night out fit the criteria. (For reference, please see any paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton or Nicole Richie at the time.) Bonus points if it could be worn underneath a blazer for the day-to-night transition from the office to the club. While the going-out top had a long dormant period as Gen Z began dressing down to go out — or not going to the club at all — it has been making a steady comeback. Skarsgård is carrying the torch with a look fitting for six vodka sodas on a weeknight before triumphantly making it back into work the next morning. It’s both dapper and elegant, true to the sex appeal of Tom Ford, and is actually one of his more subtle options when compared to say, the time he wore no pants at all. The stylist behind the Tom Ford look is Harry Lambert, who has also worked with Harry Styles, Jacob Elordi and Josh O’Connor — male stars who have all embraced a more expansive and delightful sense of masculinity in the ways that they dress. Since he began collaborating with Skarsgård, Lambert has often played up his 6’4” frame, subverting his proportions with gigantic thigh high boots, muscle-bearing halter tops, or itty-bitty short shorts. After all, why can’t a man built like a Viking have a bit of fun with what he wears? They’ve had plenty to work with based on the actors’ endless, eclectic roles, from the leather-daddy romance “Pillion” to the basket-weaving erotica “Wicker,” which launched a thousand think pieces on the uh, logistics of having a rattan-woven man as one’s lover. Since his breakout role in the vampiric love triangle “True Blood,” the actor was fated to become a sex symbol, though he’s done so with unconventional roles and a fearless sense of style to match. His willingness to poke fun at his masculinity is part of the charm. Menswear has been having a renaissance as many male celebrities have been keen to park the plain, stuffy suits and embrace styling that for too long, has only been considered feminine. After all, what’s more appealing than someone who is confident enough in who they are, and isn’t bound by gendered dress codes? Skarsgård may be one of Hollywood’s top male leads, but he’s also quite all right with being one of the girls.

He also made a statement in his “Baby” shirt by JW Anderson.

articles.title: At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
articles.summary: Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs as students and teachers say little has improved.
articles.body:
Paris, France – On a cold, rainy morning in early November, students and teachers met outside the locked gates of Paul Eluard, a high school in Saint-Denis north of Paris. Some were wearing costumes. For 17-year-old Kamelia, dressing as a dinosaur helped her to maintain the joy and hope that coexisted with the anger driving the student movement in mid-September.

“Costumes are the fun part. They show that it’s not all about violence. There’s also good cheer and fun in all of this,” Kamelia told Al Jazeera. “Today there are huge protests all over France, and it’s very important. I got up early, and even though I’m a little tired, I came anyway.”

Four days after students at Paul Eluard returned from a mid-term break, they joined a national strike on November 5. Nearby, students from the trade school Bartholdi had blockaded the gates of their school. Although the size of the student protests peaked in early October, many young people, especially in the suburbs, are refusing to return to the classroom until some of their demands are met.

“Sometimes, we see rats in the courtyard and in the restrooms. The restrooms are a mess. We don’t have enough water; it flows very slowly. We don’t have enough to drink, and the restrooms are dirty. The hallways are dirty, the classrooms are dirty, and there are cockroaches,” 17-year-old Nohlan, a student at Bartholdi, told Al Jazeera outside the school’s blockade.

The movement started at a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17, and rapidly spread to Saint-Denis, then the rest of France. Students blocked the entrances to their schools to protest poor classroom conditions and took to the streets.

“The movement started in the suburbs, then Paris followed suit. Now the whole world is watching us,” Kamelia said. “[In Saint-Denis], we’re basically ignored, even though we’re part of this country. But we’re here, and we are the future of this country.”

By the end of September, an estimated 400 schools across France, including some universities, had joined the student movement. Protests on October 17 in Paris saw an estimated 550,000 participants, according to the interior minister, while organisers put the number at 800,000.

Although this is not the first time in recent years that students in working-class suburbs have protested against school conditions, the scale of this year’s movement has been remarkable.

“It really started to gain momentum, and when everyone started to get involved, it was incredible. It really moved me because last year, we set up a few blockades, but no one heard about them,” Kamelia said.

Although students are at the heart of the movement, many teachers have since joined, expressing solidarity with their students and deploring the conditions under which they have to teach.

High school students are setting the pace for the movement, said Lucie Sabze, an English teacher at Paul Eluard.

“I’m impressed by the students, their demands and their political discourse, which is very lucid and very clear,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think the scale of the movement can be explained by a growing frustration.”

Teachers at Eluard are celebrating one “victory”. They had been calling for the resignation of the head teacher, who they accused of letting an officer from France’s notoriously violent motorised antiterrorism brigade into the school to arrest a student.

On Sunday, a government agency announced Xavier Artaud had stepped down “as a safety precaution”.

“Given the unacceptable public accusations made against the high school principal by name, he requested protective measures requiring his removal from the Saint-Denis area,” said the Academic Director of National Education Services.

Bruno Gbalou, an English teacher at neighbouring Bartholdi, noted that conditions have only deteriorated in recent years.

“It’s been about 15 years since I came back from England and started teaching here, and things have only gotten worse. So there are more students, but we have fewer resources,” Bruno Gbalou told Al Jazeera. “It’s not fair to the students, and it’s not fair to us, and that’s one of the reasons why we’re going on strike.”

In a statement to the media in early October, President Emmanuel Macron said the government planned to respond to students’ demands “in the most concrete way possible”.

“I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger, that our youth can have, whether about the climate, technological changes or geopolitical situations,” Macron said.

But the students who spoke to Al Jazeera said they do not believe the government has offered them real solutions. The November blockade at Bartholdi in Saint-Denis was in response to a lack of solutions, said student Nohlan.

“There’s still no change. We’re hoping for change, but we’re waiting, and waiting,” he said.

Louis Boyard, a member of the French National Assembly for Val-de-Marne, the administrative area where the protest movement started, explained that the government’s policies have significantly reduced educational resources.

“Macron pursued a policy of austerity, and as a result, he gradually dismantled public education while providing massive subsidies to the private sector because he supports private education over public education,” Boyard told Al Jazeera. “Macron thinks that by sweeping the problem under the rug, people will just go home. That’s not true. The people speaking out can’t really afford to eat any more. One in three French people are skipping meals. People – young people – have gone too far in this movement to back down now.”

The left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is currently polling about 20 percent in France’s upcoming presidential elections, has been accused of weaponising the student movement for political gain. But Boyard insisted that the movement was organic, and that LFI had simply followed because the party is “always on the side of those who fight”.

“Whenever there’s a struggle led by young people, I participate because I believe that young people have every right to get involved and fight,” Boyard said. “The movement took off because all the high school students looked at each other and said: ‘We’re not being respected. So we’re going to make sure we’re respected’.”

When he was a high school student, Boyard participated in a blockade, prompted by an asbestos problem, in 2018. Thanks to the protests, the students were able to get the school rebuilt.

“I’ve already won a victory this way, and we were justified in doing it. [The current students], too, are justified in doing it,” Boyard said.

As she inflated her dinosaur costume to join the protests in the centre of Paris, Kamelia wanted to send a message of hope.

“Everyone is rising up – all the young people. We’re a generation who’s truly awakened. It makes me so happy,” she said.
